Proposition 218
Given the requirements of what is commonly referred to as Proposition 218, a process must be
utilized in order to adopt and implement a change in the City’s saltwater rates. The first
requirement is that the proposed rates must be cost-based or justified and that is the reason the
City has developed the Study. Once the cost basis for the proposed saltwater rates have been
calculated, a public notice process must be undertaken in order to move forward with the
adoption of the proposed rates. This begins with the presentation of the proposed rates to the
City Council. If the proposed rates are acceptable and prudent, the City Council can direct staff
to prepare and mail the Proposition 218 notices to the City’s customers which outlines the
changes in saltwater rates and the time, date, and location of the public hearing.

The City held the public hearing for the saltwater rate study on May 19th, 2026 at
5:00pm. At the public hearing, the protest votes were counted and absent a majority of 50% +
1, the City Council was able to adopt the Study, unanimously. At a later date, the proposed
saltwater rates, not to exceed the rates as noticed to customers, will be brought forward to the
City Council for adoption and will be implemented for the next fiscai year starting July 1, 2026.

1.3 Generally Accepted Rate Setting Principles
As a practical matter, utilities should consider setting their rates around generally accepted or
global principles and guidelines. Utility rates should be:
  •  Cost-based and proportional
  •  Easy to understand and administer
  •  Designed to conform with generally accepted rate setting techniques
  •  Stable in their ability to provide adequate revenues for meeting the utility’s financial,
  operating, and regulatory requirements
  •  Established at a level that is stable from year-to-year from a customer’s perspective
  •  Established in compliance with State law

1.4 Determining the Revenue Requirement
Most public utilities use the cash basis’ approach for establishing their revenue requirement and
setting rates. This approach conforms to most public utility budgetary requirements and the
calculation is easy to understand and determine. A public utility:
  •  Totals its cash expenditures for a period of time to determine required revenues based
  on the cost of service the utility provides
  •  Adds operation and maintenance (O&M) expenses. Operation and maintenance expenses
  include the materials, electricity, labor, supplies, etc. needed to keep the utility
  functioning.

recoded when cash is disbursed.

  improvements financed with rate revenues. In lieu of including capital improvements

Under the cash basis approach, the sum of the capital and operating expenses equals the utility’s
revenue requirement during any period of time (see Table 1 2).  -

2.1.4.1  Rate Funding
A general financial guideline states that, at a minimum, a utility should fund an amount equal to
or greater than annual depreciation through rates. Annual depreciation expense reflects the
current investment in saltwater plant being depreciated or “losing” its useful life. Therefore, this
portion of plant investment needs to be replaced to maintain the existing level of infrastructure.
While the general financial guideline suggests funding an amount at least equal to the
depreciation expense, consideration should also be given to funding within rates some amount
greater than the annual depreciation expense to reflect the cost of replacement. Annual
depreciation expense reflects the cost of infrastructure that was constructed, on average, 15 to
20 years ago. Funding for the replacement cost is prudent and minimizes costs/rates over time.
As a point of reference, the City’s current annual depreciation expense for the saltwater system
is approximately $52,000 as provided in the City’s financial records for FY 2024-25. The City has
made commitments recently to cash fund capital projects. As a result, rate funded capital is
increased from $150,000 in FY 2025-26 to $350,000 in FY 2030-31 and averages $250,000 per
year over the review period.

2.1.4.2  Reserve Funding
Available reserve funds are another method of funding capital improvements. Reserve funds are
typically funded by annual surpluses or strategic planning to proactively enhance reserve
balances. This allows the City to reserve funds for projects in later years when more or larger
projects are undertaken. This approach helps to mitigate future rate adjustments and smooth
rates overtime. During the review period, approximately $692,000 in available reserves are used
to fund capital projects. Over the planning horizon, close attention should be given to the reserve
balance as to not reduce fund balances below minimum targets described below.

2.1.4.3  Long-Term Debt
Another potential funding source for capital projects is the issuance of long-term debt. While
there are certain advantages and disadvantages with the issuance of long-term debt, it is
important to weigh them when deciding whether to issue or not. Long-term debt is typically not
issued to fund renewal and replacement projects similar to those being proposed during this time
period. Rather, long-term debt is often issued for major capital projects which have an immediate
impact on rates and long-term debt is a financing mechanism to smoothly finance/fund the major
capital project. For this analysis, there is no assumed new debt issuances over the review period
of FY 2025-26 through FY 2030-3 1.

The final step of the City’s comprehensive saltwater rate study is the design of proposed rates to
collect the appropriate levels of revenues, based on the results of both the revenue requirement
and the cost of service analyses. In developing the City’s proposed saltwater rates, consideration
is given to the level of the rates as well as the structure of the rates. The level of rates reflects
the amount of revenues that should be collected while the structure of the rates is how it is
collected (i.e., component charges) from the customers.

The overall revenue level for the City’s has been established in the revenue requirement analysis
(Section 2) while the proportional distribution of costs has been developed in the cost of service
analysis (Section 3) which provides the revenue levels to be collected based on cost causation
and the cost basis for each rate component.

4.1 Rate Design Criteria and Considerations
Prudent rate administration dictates that several criteria that are considered when setting utility
rates. Some of these rate design criteria are listed below:
  •  Rates which are easy to understand from the customer’s perspective
  •  Rates which are easy for the City to administer
  •  Cost-based and proportional
  •  Continuity, overtime, of the rate making philosophy
  •  Provide revenue stability from month to month and year to year
  •  Proportional and non-discriminatory (cost-based)
  •  Meet the requirements of Proposition 218
Given the requirement and intent of Proposition 218, the last consideration, cost-based rates,
should be of paramount importance and provide the primary guidance to utilities on rate
structure and policy. When developing the proposed rate designs, all the above-listed criteria can
be taken into consideration. However, it should be noted that it is difficult, if not impossible, to
design a rate that meets all the goals and objectives listed above. In designing rates, there are
always trade-offs between the goals and objectives and a delicate balance must always be struck.

The establishment of cost-based and proportional rates was of paramount importance in the
development of the City’s saltwater rate study. Meeting the requirements and documenting the
steps taken to develop cost-based and proportional rates has been in the forefront with the legal
challenges in the State of California on utility rates. A focus has been given to meeting the
requirements of California Constitution article XIII D, section 6 (Article XIII D). A key component
of Article XIII D is the development of rates which reflect the cost of providing service and are
proportionally distributed between the customer classes of service, and the customers within
each class. HDR would point out that there is no single methodology for proportionally assigning
costs to the customer classes. The Water Environment Federation Manual of Practice #27
provides methodologies which may be used to establish cost-based rates. Unfortunately, Article
XIII D is not prescriptive and does not provide a specific methodology for establishing cost-based
rates.

 HDR is of the opinion that the proposed rates meet the legal requirements of Article XIII D. HDR
reaches this conclusion based upon the following:
  •  The revenue derived from saltwater rates does not exceed the funds required to
  provide the property related service (i.e., saltwater service). The proposed rates are
  designed to collect the overall revenue requirement of the City’s saltwater system.
  •  The revenues derived from saltwater rates shall not be used for any purpose other than
  that for which the fee or charge is imposed. The revenues derived from the City’s
  saltwater rates are used exclusively to fund the City’s saltwater system O&M and provide
  adequate funding for capital improvement, repair, and replacement.
  •  The amount of a fee or charge imposed upon a parcel or person as an incident of
  property ownership shall not exceed the proportional costs of the service attributable
  to the parcel. The Study has appropriately grouped customers into customer classes of
  service (residential, etc.) that reflect the customer usage patterns and system
  requirements (i.e., the benefits they receive from and burdens they place on the system)
  of each customer class of service. The grouping of customers and rates into these classes
  of service creates the proportionality expected under Article XIII D by having differing
  rates by customer classes of service which reflect both the level of revenue to be collected
  by the utility, and the manner in which these costs are incurred and assigned to customer
  classes of service based upon their proportional impacts.

1.3 Generally Accepted Rate Setting Principles
As a practical matter, utilities should set rates around generally accepted or global principles and
guidelines. Utility rates should be:
  •  Cost-based and proportional
  •  Easy to understand and administer
  •  Designed to conform with generally accepted rate setting techniques
  •  Stable in their ability to provide adequate revenues for meeting the utility’s financial,
  operating, and regulatory requirements
  •  Established at a level that is stable from year-to-year from a customer’s perspective
  •  Established in compliance with State and local legislative requirements

1.4 Determining the Revenue Requirement
Most public utilities use the cash basis’ approach for establishing the revenue requirement and
setting rates. This approach conforms to most public utility budgetary requirements and the
calculation is easy to understand and determine. A public utility:
  •  Totals its cash expenditures for a period of time to determine required revenues based
  on the cost of service the utility provides
  •  Adds operation and maintenance (O&M) expenses. Operation and maintenance
  expenses include the materials, electricity, labor, supplies, etc. needed to keep the utility
  functioning.
  •  Calculates capital costs by adding debt service payments (principal and interest) to
  capital improvements financed with rate revenues. In lieu of including capital
  improvements financed with rate revenues, a utility sometimes includes depreciation
  expense to stabilize annual revenue requirement.

recorded when cash is disbursed.

 Under the cash basis approach, the sum of the capital and operating expenses equals the utility’s
revenue requirement during any period of time (see Table 1- 2).

Note that the two portions of the capital expense component (debt service and capital
improvements financed from rates) are necessary under the cash basis approach because utilities
generally cannot finance all capital facilities with long-term debt. The analyses developed within
this report utilize the cash basis methodology. This is consistent with past practices in the City’s
utility rate-setting process and is the most widely accepted method of accumulating costs for
municipal utilities.

2.1.4.1  Rate Funding
A general financial guideline states that, at a minimum, a utility should fund an amount from
rates which is equal to or greater than the annual depreciation expense. Annual depreciation
expense reflects the current investment in plant being depreciated or “losing” its useful life.
Therefore, this portion of plant investment needs to be annually funded to maintain the existing
level of infrastructure. In addition, consideration should be given to using rate revenues to fund
an amount greater than the annual depreciation expense for repairs and replacements as costs
escalate over time and replacement cost is generally greater than the original cost. Whenever
possible, the City should be funding capital projects from rates in an amount greater than annual
depreciation expense to better reflect replacement costs. At the present time, the annual
depreciation expense of the solid waste utility is approximately $46,000 based on the City’s

   1  Solid Waste Cost of Service
In the previous section, the revenue requirement analysis focused on the total revenues required
to adequately fund the City’s solid waste utility. This section will provide an overview of the
second step in a comprehensive solid waste rate study; the cost of service analysis developed for
the City’s solid waste utility.

The objective of the cost of service analysis is different from determining the revenue
requirement. Whereas the revenue requirement analysis determines the utility’s overall revenue
needs, the cost of service analysis determines the proportional distribution of the revenue
requirement to establish proposed rates for the proposed time period. In this case, the revenue
requirement for FY 2026-27, the first year of the proposed rate transition plan, was used for
establishing the cost of service analysis.

3.1 Objectives of a Cost of Service Analysis
There are two primary objectives in conducting a cost of service analysis:
  •  Proportionally distribute the City’s solid waste revenue requirement, and
  •  Derive the cost basis for subsequent rate designs by customer class of service
The objectives of the cost of service analysis are different from determining a revenue
requirement. As noted in the previous section, a revenue requirement analysis determines the
utility’s overall financial needs, while the cost of service analysis determines the proportional
manner to collect the calculated revenue requirement.

3.2 Development of the Solid Waste Cost of Service

Consequently, the City does not have information available on customers in regards to the size
of the solid waste container, the frequency of service for each customers, or the number of pick

service to the City’s customers is unavailable. It should also be noted that information on actual
waste generation by customer type is limited, as most collection and disposal practices do not
separate by customer type in a similar way to how the City charges for solid waste service. For
example, a utility typically does not have information on the average tonnage collected from an

   4 Solid Waste Rate Design
The final step of the City’s comprehensive solid waste rate study is the design of proposed rates
to collect the appropriate levels of revenues, based on the results of both the revenue
requirement and the cost of service analyses. In developing the City’s proposed solid waste rates,
consideration is given to the level of the rates as well as the structure of the rates. The level of
rates reflects the amount of revenues that should be collected while the structure of the rates is
how it is collected (i.e., component charges) from the customers.

4.1 Rate Design Criteria and Considerations
Prudent rate administration dictates that several criteria should be considered when setting
utility rates. Some of these rate design criteria are listed below:
  •  Rates which are easy to understand from the customer’s perspective
  •  Rates which are easy for the City to administer
  •  Consideration of the customer’s ability to pay
  •  Cost-based
  •  Provide revenue stability from month to month and year to year
  •  Proportional and non-discriminatory (cost-based)
  •  Defensible (Proposition 218 compliant)
Given the requirement and intent of Proposition 218, the last consideration, cost-based rates,
should be of paramount importance and provide the primary guidance to utilities on rate
structure and policy.

The establishment of cost-based and proportional solid waste rates was of paramount
importance in the development of the City’s Study. Meeting the requirements and documenting
the steps taken to develop cost-based and proportional rates has been in the forefront of
meeting the requirements of California Constitution article XIII D, section 6. A key component of
Article XIII D is the development of rates which reflect the cost of providing service and are
proportionally distributed between the customer classes of service, and the customers within
each class. HDR would point out that there is no single methodology for proportionally assigning
costs to the customer classes. Unfortunately, Article XIII D is not prescriptive and does not
provide a specific methodology for establishing cost-based rates.

HDR is of the opinion that the proposed rates meet the legal requirements of Article XIII D. HDR
reaches this conclusion based upon the following:
  •  The revenue derived from solid waste rates does not exceed the funds required to
  provide the property related service (i.e., solid waste service). The proposed rates are
  designed to collect the overall revenue requirement of the City’s solid waste utility.
  •  The revenues derived from solid waste rates shall not be used for any purpose other
  than that for which the fee or charge is imposed. The revenues derived from the City’s
  solid waste rates are used exclusively to fund the City’s solid waste utility O&M and
  provide adequate funding for capital improvement, repair, and replacement of the solid
  waste facilities.

 4.4 Proposition 218
Given the requirements of what is commonly referred to as Proposition 218, a process must be
utilized in order to adopt and implement a change in the City’s solid waste rates. The first
requirement is that the proposed rates must be cost-based or justified and that is the reason the
City has developed the Study. Once the cost basis for the proposed solid waste rates have been
calculated, a public notice process must be undertaken in order to move forward with the
adoption of the proposed rates. This begins with the presentation of the proposed rates to the
City Council. If the proposed rates are acceptable and prudent, the City Council can direct staff
to prepare and mail the Proposition 218 notices to the City’s customers which outlines the
changes in solid waste rates and the time, date, and location of the public hearing.

The City held the public hearing for the solid waste rate study on May 19th, 2026 at
5:00pm. At the public hearing, the protest votes were counted and absent a majority of 50% +
1, the City Council was able to adopt the Study, unanimously. At a later date, the proposed solid
waste rates, not to exceed the rates as noticed to customers, will be brought forward to the City
Council for adoption and will be implemented for the next fiscal year starting July 1, 2026.

SUBJECT:  Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Hear a presentation regarding the Miscellaneous Fee
Schedule. 2. Open the Public Hearing to hear public comments. 3. Close the Public Hearing. 4.
If consensus, adopt the fee schedule as proposed.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City charges fees for miscellaneous public services, use of City
facilities and equipment rental and other activities. User fees are assessed and collected for City
services and programs provided by various departments. These are services that convey a
benefit, grant a privilege, provide for review and enforcement of regulatory activities, enforce
laws, or are a condition of development. Under state law, cities may charge fees to recoup the
direct and indirect costs related to the provision of user services.

Each year, the City reviews its fees to establish new fees, modify existing fees, and eliminate
fees that are no longer required to ensure that City fees are in-line with the costs incurred to
provide them.

In Fiscal Year 2025-2026, City Council approved a 3.12% increase for the majority of fees, with
the exception of transit and certain recreation fees. The percentage increase was based on the
consumer price index (CPI) information provided by the Bureau of Labor Statistics for Los
Angeles County based on the latest available fiscal year information. Using the CPI as an
average cost increase annually ensures the city does not unnecessarily burden the citizens with
unusually large spikes in fees while also ensuring that the City continues to recoup costs
associated with the increased costs to provide these services.

For Fiscal Year 2026-2027, Staff recommends increasing the majority of fees based on the latest
available calendar year consumer price index (CPI) information provided by the Bureau of Labor
Statistics for Los Angeles County which shows an increase of 3.12% based for the fiscal year
average for 2025, with the fees rounded to the nearest dollar.

As part of its review process, City Staff is proposing to not increase certain fees related to
recreation and transit, with those services to be further subsidized with general tax revenues,
with the exception of Tremont Hall, which was increased from $125 to $150 for a full-day resident
private use to cover the increased maintenance and capital improvements to the building over
the last fiscal year. The City also updated ambulance service rates to align with the County of
Los Angeles General Public Ambulance rates effective July 1, 2026.
 The City added a new Code Enforcement fee for Electric Bicycle Release Fee of $100. The
existing release fees of $200 for vehicles and $25 for bicycles will remain unchanged.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: City costs will be offset by annual revenues.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Staff estimates that the new City fees, if adopted as proposed, should
generate approximately $5,000  $10,000 in new General Fund revenues, primarily from
  -

Planning-related fees, and $70,000 in additional Harbor Fund revenues, primarily from nightly
moorings.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The costs of special
services will not be fully funded through fees paid by the users of those services. The unfunded
portion of user services would then be subsidized by general tax revenues and/or available fund
balances.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Adopt the attached resolution establishing city rates and fees for
services.

SUBJECT:  Catalina Food Tours Transportation Permit Application

RECOMMENDED ACTION: 1. Receive presentation. 2. Discuss. 3. If consensus is met,
approve the Transportation Permit for Catalina Food Tours to be added to the existing
Residential Vehicle permit to conduct tours with stated conditions.

REPORT SUMMARY: On April 26, 2026 the City received a transportation permit application
from Ms. Erin Eubank to conduct guided food tours utilizing one existing Residential Vehicle
permit assigned to business partner Simon Alvarez. The existing company is a walking tour and
would like to add a transportation component for local restaurants further out from town center.

The proposed Residential Vehicle permit would be used to conduct in-town tours and tours into
the interior as outlined in the map attached between the hours of 9:00 am and 7:00 pm with the
primary pick-up and drop-off at the intersection of Metropole and Crescent in the Passenger
Loading Zone. Additional drop-off locations include Descanso Beach Club, Buffalo Nickel,
Avalon Smokehouse, Sand Trap, and Airport in the Sky (pending approval).

Avalon Municipal Code Section (AMC) §5-14.04 requires a hearing before the City Council to
determine whether a transportation permit should be approved ensuring:
  • The applicant has presented facts demonstrating a necessity for the requested vehicle(s).
  • The requested vehicle(s) is appropriate for the intended use and necessary, for the proper
  functioning of the applicant’s enterprise.
  • The requested vehicle(s) will not have a deleterious impact on traffic congestion, traffic
  safety, noise, or air pollution.
  • In view of the size and nature of the streets of the City and the character of the City itself,
  the requested vehicle(s) will not have a deleterious impact on the public health, safety,
  and welfare.
  • There is no more suitable alternative vehicle than the vehicle(s) requested by the
  applicant that can satisfy its requirements.

If approved by the City Council, staff recommends the applicant must additionally meet the
following conditions:
   •  Agree to limit primary pick-up and drop-off locations to the passenger loading zone of
  Crescent Avenue/Metropole Avenue.
  •  Agree to limit in-town secondary pick-up and drop-off locations to include Descanso
  Beach Club, Buffalo Nickel, Avalon Smokehouse, and Sand Trap.
  •  Agree to limit transportation hours to 9:00am to 7:00pm, seven days a week.
  •  Agree to limit vehicle parking to a maximum of 5 minutes to allow for the active
  loading/unloading of passengers, never leaving the vehicle unattended.
  •  Maintain an active City of Avalon business license.
  •  Maintain current City of Avalon Residential Vehicle permit.
  Maintain current on City of Avalon Admissions Tax payments.
  •  Provide proof of insurance per the Avalon Municipal Code.
  Ensure approval from any private entities for private road use if applicable.
  •  Failure to fully comply with any of the foregoing conditions shall result in the revocation
  of the applicant’s transportation permit.

Renewals to be evaluated by the Vehicle Clerk to ensure compliance every three years.

FISCAL IMPACTS: None.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: N/A

SUBJECT:  Adult-Use Cannabis Discussion

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Provide direction to Staff regarding City Council’s desire to
pursue legalization of adult-use cannabis in Avalon.

REPORT SUMMARY: This item appears on the agenda at the request of a member of the City
Council. Over the last several years cannabis has appeared on Council’s agenda for
discussion or action on seven occasions.

  August 6, 2024: City Council Meeting. Council affirms City Manager’s decision to
  terminate the existing, but inactive, medical cannabis delivery permit. Discussion held
  regarding expanding cannabis regulations and accepting applications to re-issue the
  medical delivery permit.

  September 17, 2024: City Council Meeting. City Staff provided a feasibility analysis
  regarding a store front adult-use facHity, the community’s desire/interest in the facility,
  and projected economic and other impacts

  January 21, 2025: City Council Meeting. Council again discusses options for cannabis
  in Avalon and authorizes staff to resolicit applications for the issuance of the medical
  cannabis delivery permit.

  May 6, 2025: City Council conducts a Public Hearing and adopts a Resolution declaring
  an intent to award the medical cannabis delivery permit to Catalina Cannabis, LLC.

  August 5, 2025: City Council adopted Resolution No. 25-27 issuing a commercial
  cannabis permit to Catalina Cannabis, [[C for Medical Delivery Business. (On August
  19, 2025, City Staff was notified Catalina Cannabis, LLC changed to ERBA Catalina, a
  California C-corporation.)

  October 21, 2025: City Council directed City Staff to not pursue legalization of adult
  use/recreational cannabis in Avalon.

  April 21, 2026: City Council heard a presentation from ERBA Catalina  the current
  —

  medical cannabis delivery business permit holder  regarding adult-use/recreational
  —

  cannabis. Representatives of ERBA requested Council’s consideration to amend the
   current medical delivery ordinance to allow them to also deliver adult-use recreational
  cannabis. Because the electorate has never approved adult-use recreational delivery
  and therefore there is no provision for a tax, ERBA proposed a development agreement
  with the City offering payment of five percent (5%) of their gross receipts. City Council
  directed City Staff to bring an item back for further discussion and consideration.

Development of Local Cannabis Regulations and Public Interest in Adult-Use Cannabis

After the establishment of state-wide legislation regarding cannabis, acting in accordance with
its local jurisdictional authority under MAUCRSA, the Avalon City Council began the process to
develop its local ordinance. After discussions and code revisions at four City Council meetings,
the current cannabis ordinance (Ordinance #1163-17, Chapter 5-20 of the AMC) was adopted
on November 7, 2017.

In development of Ordinance #1163-17, the City Council worked to provide a means for public
access to medical cannabis by supporting a medical cannabis business delivery process, while
protecting the City’s neighborhoods, residents and businesses from potential negative impacts.
Additionally, the City Council took steps to minimize the potential impact of cannabis business
in Avalon by:

  -  Requiring any medical cannabis delivery service business to locate their brick-and-
  mortar place of business within the City’s commercial or special commercial zones.
  -  Prohibiting signage on the exterior of the brick-and-mortar facility identifying it as a
  commercial cannabis business.
  -  Requiring extensive odor control devices and techniques be implemented.
  -  Requiring extensive security measures including 24-hour video surveillance, and
  uniformed personnel on site.
  -  Limiting medical cannabis delivery services permits to just one in the first year of
  operation.

At the request of the City Council, the City of Avalon added two advisory measures to the
March 3, 2020 General Municipal Election ballot.

Measure E asked: “Should the City of Avalon expand its current commercial cannabis
ordinance from medical delivery only to allow for adult-use/recreational delivery sales within
the City of Avalon city limits?”

  -  58.45% or 612 voters voted “No” against expansion of the ordinance to allow adult
  use/recreational delivery.

  -  41 .55% or 435 voters voted “Yes” in favor of expansion of the ordinance to allow adult
  use/recreational delivery.

Measure F asked: “Should the City of Avalon expand its current commercial cannabis
ordinance to allow for a cannabis storefront location or dispensary within the City of Avalon city
limits?”
   -  65.14% or 682 voters voted “No” against expansion of the ordnance to allow a
  cannabis storefront.

  -  34.86% or 365 voters voted “Yes” in favor of expansion of the ordinance to allow for a
  cannabis storefront.

Since the advisory measures, City Staff have not received any significant request or call for
expansion of the cannabis ordinance from the public at large. Additionally, the medical
cannabis delivery permit was suspended from September 2021 to 2025. During that time
period, City Staff did not receive any significant inquiries, or requests from the community at
large for the return of medical cannabis.

Options to Pursue Legalization of Adult-Use Cannabis

1. Direct City Staff to Place a Measure on the November 3, 2026 General Election as either
  an advisory measure or final consideration.

For example, Measure E and Measure F were both Advisory Measures that provided a clear
direction at the time that the residents were not in favor of either recreational delivery or
storefront dispensary. In reliance on the results of these two advisory measures, City Council
did not pursue either path.

Additionally, on November 8, 2016, a citizen referendum was placed on a Special Election for
the consideration of Measure X. Measure X asked: “Shall the Avalon Municipal Code he
amended to permit up to two medical marijuana dispensaries and similar facilities, both fixed
and mobile, operate within the City, and to permit the cultivation, manufacture and processing
of medical marijuana products, subject to specified standards, and further subject to a $10,000
annual license tax and a 12% transaction fee/tax on each individual medical marijuana sale
until repealed by voters, and generating approximately $200,000 annually?”

  -  63% or 721 voted “No”.
  -  36% or 421 voted “Yes”.

City Council may request an advisory measure to appear on a ballot as was done in 2020, or
for a ballot measure enacting the proposed changes to the Avalon Municipal Code and
establishing a tax as was done in 2016.

The deadline for a local jurisdictional ballot measure to appear on the November 3, 2026
General Election ballot either by citizen referendum or City Council direction is August 7,
  —  —

2026.

Additionally, even if a ballot measure is approved, it is not clear that Council would be
authorized to award a newly created recreational adult-use permit to the previously existing
medical delivery permit holder or open the new permit up for applications.

2. Amend the Avalon Municipal Code and Direct City Staff and City Attorney to Draft a
  Development Agreement with the Existing Permit Holder
 ERBA has proposed City Council amend Chapter 5-20 of the AMC to allow for adult-
use/recreational cannabis delivery and enter into a development agreement setting forth a 5%
fee of all of ERBA’s gross sales to be remitted to the City annually.

The City Council may amend the AMC; and a fee could be established through a development
agreement. Setting a fee via a development agreement creates more risk to the City than a
voter approved tax/fee The State of California Government Code Section 66000-66008
establishes rules for how local agencies can establish, set, and use fees. An established fee
should reflect cost of services or the direct impact to offset use of public facilities. While a fee
agreed upon through the negotiation of a development agreement is defensible, it imposes
more risk than a voter approved tax/fee.

Further, if the AMC is amended to allow recreational cannabis delivery, the City Council may
want allow competition for such a vendor rather than extending the use to the current operator
of the medical delivery service.
An additional consideration is whether modifying the AMC and entering into a Development
Agreement fee would subject the City Council to arguments that it is circumventing the prior
voter decisions to reject the expansion of cannabis in Avalon as reflected in the previous ballot
measures.

PREPARED BY:  Devin Hart, Management Analyst

SUBJECT:  Adult Use Cannabis Feasibility Discussion

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Hear presentation. If consensus is reached, provide direction
to Staff.

REPORT SUMMARY: A member of the City Council requested City Staff bring a report before
the City Council considering expansion of the Avalon Municipal Code to include Adult-Use
Cannabis. Specifically, the Councilmember requested Staff research and provide an analysis
regarding a store front adult-use facility, the community’s desire/interest in the facility, and
projected economic and other impacts.

Legal Framework
Though the use of medical cannabis was legalized in the State of California in 1996, adult-use
or recreational cannabis was prohibited until adoption of Proposition 64 on November 8, 2016.
On June 27, 2017, Governor Jerry Brown signed into law a single comprehensive legislative
document that took the existing regulatory framework established for medical cannabis and
incorporated non-medical cannabis regulations. This legislation is known as the Medicinal and
Adult-Use Cannabis Regulation and Safety Act (“MAUCRSA”). The legislation specifically
preserved local jurisdictional authority to adopt and enforce local ordinances that limit or
completely prohibit the establishment or operation of medical and non-medical cannabis
business operations within their purview. The state licensing authority will not approve an
application for a state cannabis business license if the state license will violate a local
ordinance in the jurisdiction it will operate.

The Department of Cannabis Control Medicinal and Adult-Use Commercial Cannabis
Regulations  —  California Code of Regulations Title 4 Division 19 Section §15311,
“Requirements for the Transportation of Cannabis and Cannabis Products” establishes the
  —

requirements for transporting cannabis and cannabis products between licensees or licensed
premises.

Though regulation §153111 (e) expressly prohibits transportation of cannabis and cannabis
products “by means of aircraft, watercraft, drone, rail, human-powered vehicle, or unstaffed
vehicle,” a carve out exits for Catalina within Section (p):

  Notwithstanding subsection (e), transportation of cannabis and cannabis products may
  be conducted via waterway to licensees located on Catalina island. The provisions of
  this section and other sections regarding vehicle requirements also apply to vessels
   used to transport cannabis and cannabis products via wateiway pursuant to this
  section.

Cannabis is an illegal substance under the Federal Controlled Substances Act, 21 USC et.
seq., (“Act”) which makes it unlawful for any person to cultivate, manufacture, distribute or
dispense, or possess with intent to manufacture, distribute or dispense cannabis. The Act does
not contain any exemption for cannabis used for medical purposes. Additionally, per federal
law, cannabis is listed as a Schedule 1 drug. Federal penalties for possession of cannabis
include:
  -  First Offense —  Misdemeanor with potential for up to one year of incarceration and
  $1,000 in fines.
  -  Second Offense  —  Misdemeanor punishable by 15 days to two years of incarceration
  and $2,500 in fines.
  -  Third and subsequent Offenses  —  Misdemeanor or felony punishable by 90 days to 3
  years of incarceration and fines up to $2,500.

Federal penalties increase significantly for selling or attempting to sell cannabis based on the
amount:
  -  Less than 50 kilograms  Felony punishable by up to five years in prison and a
  —

  $250,000 fine
  -  50 to 99 kilograms Felony punishable by up to 20 years in prison and fines of up to
  —

  $1,000,000.
  -  100 to 999 kilograms  Felony punishable by five to 40 years in prison and possible
  —

  fines of up to $2,000,000.
  -  1000 kg and up  — Felony punishable by ten years to life in prison and $4,000,000 in
  fines.

However, it should be noted, federal law enforcement agencies have issued guidelines
allowing for state regulatory policies that include cannabis for medical purposes. Specifically,
the Rohrabaher-Farr Amendment, first introduced to the U.S. House of Representatives in
2001 and adopted in an omnibus spending bill in December 2014, prohibits the U.S. Justice
Department from spending any funds on actions designed to interfere with the state medical
cannabis laws. To date, this provision has been included in every subsequent spending bill.

Rohrabacher-Farr Amendment states:

  None of the funds made available in this Act to the Department of Justice may be used,
  with respect to the States of Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado,
  Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Hawaii, Illinois, Iowa, Kentucky,
  Maine, Matyland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississipp Missouri, Montana,
  Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, South
  Carolina, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin, to prevent such
  States from implementing their own State laws that authorize the use, distribution,
  possession, or cultivation of medical marijuana.
 The Rohrabacher-Farr Amendment is vitally important for the City of Avalon’s medical
cannabis program as the surrounding Pacific Ocean falls within the jurisdictional authority of
the United States Coast Guard (‘USCG”).

The City has received reports of medical cannabis delivery vessels being boarded by USCG.
As the vessel, medical cannabis and medical cannabis products have had all of the required
documentation for certified medical use, no action was taken by the USCG. The Harbormaster
contacted the USCG who confirmed, adult-use cannabis transportation in federal waterways is
illegal.

Though, state regulation §153111 (p) does not distinguish between medical or adult-use
cannabis in is regulatory carve out for Catalina Island, the Rohrabacher-Farr Amendment is
specific in its guidance to restrict funding for interference with State permitted medical
cannabis operations. No federal protections, exemptions or guidelines exist for adult-
use/recreational cannabis. When state law and federal law conflict, federal law displaces or
preempts state law. Therefore, City Staff interpret there is no viable way to transport adult-use
cannabis to Catalina Island without violating federal law (transportation of a controlled
substance) and/or risking the federal penalties as described within this report.

The Department of Justice has proposed a rule change to move cannabis from Schedule I to
Schedule III controlled substance. The rule change emphasizes the currently accepted medical
use of cannabis, but, again, does not address adult use. If the rule change occurs,
transportation of cannabis across federal waterways will still be prohibited.

Development of Local Cannabis Regulations and Public Interest in Adult-Use Cannabis

After the establishment of state-wide legislation regarding cannabis, acting in accordance with
its local jurisdictional authority under MAUCRSA, the Avalon City Council began the process to
develop its local ordinance. After discussions and code revisions at four City Council meetings,
the current cannabis ordinance (Ordinance #1163-17, Chapter 5-20 of the AMC) was adopted
on November 7, 2017.

In development of Ordinance #1163-17, the City Council worked to provide a means for public
access to medical cannabis by supporting a medical cannabis business delivery process, while
protecting the City’s neighborhoods, residents and businesses from potential negative impacts.
Additionally, the City Council took steps to minimize the potential impact of cannabis business
in Avalon by:
  -  Requiring any medical cannabis delivery service business to locate their brick and
  mortar place of business within the City’s commercial or special commercial zones.
  -  Prohibiting signage on the exterior of the brick and mortar facility identifying it as a
  commercial cannabis business.
  -  Requiring extensive odor control devices and techniques be implemented.
  -  Requiring extensive security measures including 24 hour video surveillance, and
  uniformed personnel on site.
  -  Limiting medical cannabis delivery services permits to just one in the first year of
  operation.
 At the request of the City Council, the City of Avalon added two advisory measures to the
March 3, 2020 General Municipal Election ballot.

Measure F asked: “Should the City of Avalon expand its current commercial cannabis
ordinance from medical delivery only to allow for adult-use/recreational delivery sales within
the City of Avalon city limits?”
  -  58.45% or 612 voters voted “No” against expansion of the ordinance to allow adult-
  use/recreational delivery.
  -  41 .55% or 435 voters voted “Yes” in favor of expansion of the ordinance to allow adult-
  use/recreational delivery.

Measure F asked: “Should the City of Avalon expand its current commercial cannabis
ordinance to allow for a cannabis storefront location or dispensary within the City of Avalon city
limits?”
  -  65.14% or 682 voters voted “No” against expansion of the ordnance to allow a cannabis
  storefront.
  -  34.86% or 365 voters voted “Yes” in favor of expansion of the ordinance to allow for a
  cannabis storefront.

Since the advisory measures, City Staff have not received any request or call from expansion
of the cannabis ordinance from the public at large. Additionally, the medical cannabis delivery
permit was suspended in September 2021. From that time to date City Staff have not received
any inquiries, outcry or requests from the community at large for medical cannabis.

Community and Economic Impact

To accurately determine the potential economic impact of expansion of the City’s cannabis
ordinance, a number of factors must be determined, including:
  -  Federal regulations regarding transport adult-use cannabis to the Island.
  -  Type of commercial cannabis facility storefront dispensary vs adult-use delivery.
  -

  -  Locations for consumption. (Currently, smoking cannabis is prohibited in public places.)
  This is a significant factor to determine as approximately 75% of the Island’s visitors are
  day trippers or from a cruise ship. These visitors would be limited in their options if they
  wanted to consume the product while in the City.
  -  Geographic isolation.
  -  Locations for brick-and-mortar commercial cannabis facilities. With limited properties,
  limited pool of property owners and currently no known vacancies in the City’s
  commercial and special commercial zones, finding an appropriate location may be
  difficult.
  -  Additional cost of enhanced enforcement and additional administrative support to
  manage commercial cannabis regulations as well as additional enforcement for
  regulation of illicit cannabis market.
  -  Rate of taxation. Adult-use cannabis and cannabis products are subject to sales tax. In
  addition, the state requires a 15% excise tax on cannabis sale gross receipts to support
  environmental cleanup, law enforcement and drug prevention programs. The City is
  able to add an additional local cannabis business tax not to exceed 15%. However, the
  rate of tax may be prohibitive to creating a thriving legal, commercial cannabis market.
   -  Other visitor driven revenue areas that may be impacted by an expanded cannabis
  ordinance. Further, any City imposed cannabis tax would have to be approved by the
  voters.

 Not accounting for the above-listed factors, City Staff conducted a survey of California cities to
provide some framework to understand and project potential cannabis revenues for Avalon.
The City’s Staff typically look to for comparison Monterrey, Morro Bay, Solvang, Oceanside,

SUBJECT:  Award to DCCM for Project Management Services

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Make the affirmative finding the City will not gain a
competitive advantage through a separate competitive solicitation and that the required
services can be obtained more economically and efficiently pursuant to Avalon Municipal
Code Section 3-4.111(C); 2. Award a Professional Services Agreement to DCCM to
provide Project Management Services for the Pebbly Beach Landfill Life Site Optimization
Project and related on-call consulting services in an amount not-to-exceed $200,000
annually; and 3. Authorize the City Manager to execute the Agreement and any related
documents, including amendments within the approved contract authority.

REPORT SUMMARY: The Pebbly Beach Landfill Life Site Optimization Project is a
critical infrastructure initiative intended to maximize the operational lifespan of the City’s
landfill facilities, improve operational efficiencies, support regulatory compliance, and
ensure continued solid waste management services for the Avalon community.

As the project advances through planning, permitting, design, environmental review, and
implementation phases, the City requires dedicated project management support to
coordinate multiple consultants, regulatory agencies, utility providers, contractors, and
stakeholders. The City had been using in-house staff for project supervision and oversight
but as the needs for the project advance additional outside professional support is
necessary to maintain project schedules and ensure successful project delivery.

On October 2, 2024, the City issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) for Building,
Engineering, and Consulting Services. The City received six proposals from qualified
firms. A selection panel reviewed the proposals based upon qualifications, relevant
experience, project approach, responsiveness to the City’s needs, and cost. Each
consultant participated in a virtual interview and presentation on November 15, 2024.

Following the evaluation process, the City Council awarded contracts to 4LEAF, Inc. and
International Consulting Services (ICS) to provide various professional services, not
including project management. At this time, City staff has identified the need for additional
project management resources to support implementation of the Pebbly Beach Landfill
Life Site Optimization Project, one of the City’s most significant capital and regulatory
compliance initiatives.
 Based on the information obtained during the City’s competitive RFP process, staff
recommends entering into a Professional Services Agreement with DCCM to provide
project management services specifically related to the Pebbly Beach Landfill Life Site
Optimization Project. DCCM was identified as one of the City’s preferred firms through
the RFP evaluation process and possesses the experience, technical expertise, and
resources necessary to assist the City with project delivery, consultant coordination,
regulatory agency communications, schedule management, grant administration support,
and other project management functions. Of the firms participating in the 2024 process,
DCCM had superior project management abilities. They were not chosen for that work
because at that time, the work would be done in house.

DCCM submitted a comprehensive proposal during the City’s 2024 REP process and was
highly rated by the evaluation panel, though not chosen for the specific work
contemplated to be done by outside vendors at that time. The firm’s proposal
demonstrated substantial experience providing project management, engineering
support, capital improvement program administration, and municipal consulting services
for local government agencies throughout California.

Staff’s evaluation identified several strengths including:
  • Extensive experience managing complex public infrastructure and environmental
  projects;
  • Demonstrated understanding of municipal operations and regulatory
  requirements;
  • Strong project controls, reporting, and stakeholder coordination capabilities;
  • Availability of qualified personnel to immediately support City needs;
  • Competitive fee structure; and
  • Positive references from public agency clients.

Following the City’s review of the 2024 process, staff contacted references provided by
DCCM. References confirmed that DCCM consistently delivered quality work products,
maintained project schedules, communicated effectively with agency staff, and provided
responsive professional services.

Awarding the proposed agreement will allow the City to maintain continuity on the Pebbly
Beach Landfill Life Site Optimization Project while providing flexibility to obtain additional
technical consulting support when needed.

Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.111(C) authorizes the City Council to make a finding
that the City will not gain a competitive advantage by bidding and that services may be
obtained more economically or efficiently through a professional services agreement.
Staff recommend that the City Council make this finding based on the following:
  • DCCM participated in the City’s competitive RFP process completed in 2024 and
  was highly rated;
  • The services are professional and specialized in nature;
  • The City has already evaluated DCCM’s qualifications, experience, staffing, and
  pricing;
   •  Immediate project management support is needed to maintain project continuity
  during staffing transitions; and
  •  Utilizing DCCM will provide a more efficient and cost-effective approach than
  conducting a new solicitation process. Maintaining project progression is critical.

The proposed agreement would be effective through December 31, 2029, with options
for future extensions subject to City approval and include additional on-call services
related to engineering plan review and inspection services to provide staff flexibility in
seeing the project through to completion.

FISCAL IMPACTS: The proposed Professional Services Agreement has a total not-to-
exceed amount of $200,000 annually. Funding is available within existing project budgets
and approved appropriations associated with the Pebbly Beach Landfill Life Site
Optimization Project and related professional services accounts.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Not applicable.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will not
have adequate resources to manage the Pebbly Beach Life Site Optimization Project and
risk not meeting tight project timelines.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Execute a professional services agreement with DCCM and hand
off project management responsibilities.

 1. Project Background
The City of Avalon (‘City”) is advancing the Pebbly Beach Landfill Life Site Optimization Project
to extend the operational life of the City’s existing landfill facility through the construction of an
approximately eighteen-foot mechanically stabilized earth (“MSE”) wall at the toe of the existing
 landfill site (roughly 5.5 acres on a 7 acre parcel). The proposed improvement is anticipated to
create vertical disposal airspace equivalent to more than twenty-seven years of additional landfill
capacity.
The City currently has less than one and one-half (1.5) years of remaining landfill capacity
available at the existing site, making timely entitlement, environmental clearance, permitting,
design, and construction implementation critical to continued solid waste operations for the
community. The site is owned by the City, operated by CR&R, and is located in an unincorporated
portion of Los Angeles County.
The City previously assigned an internal staff member to manage the project; however, that
position is expected to be vacant by June 23, 2026. The City therefore seeks consultant support
to serve as the City’s representative and owner’s project manager for the ongoing entitlement,
environmental, design, permitting, bidding, and construction coordination phases of the project.
The City has already completed substantial work on the project, including:
  • Submission of the Conditional Use Permit (“CUP”) application and SEATAC Coastal
  Development Permit (“CDP”) application to Los Angeles County Regional Planning;
  • Engagement of Geo-Logic Associates, with subconsultant Rincon Consultants, to prepare
  and submit CEQA documentation and technical studies;
  • Completion and submission of technical studies and reports supporting an Initial Study  —

  County Solid Waste Task Force to continue to proceed;
  • Ongoing coordination with County departments to address comments from GMED (in-
  progress, nearly complete);
  • Anticipated public circulation of the lS-MND in Summer 2026;
  • Ongoing preparation of engineering plans and specifications for the MSE wall by Geo
  Logic Associates to be used in bid and procurement documents (final review and approval

  • Regular bi-weekly coordination meetings among the City, Geo-Logic, Rincon, CR&R, and

SUBJECT:  Pebbly Beach Road Temporary Turn Around Installation and Traffic
  Safety Improvements

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Approve the plan as presented for modifications and striping
along Pebbly Beach Road including installation of k-rail, signage and striping to install a
temporary vehicle turn around.

REPORT SUMMARY: Due to construction associated with the Cabrillo Mole Revitalization
Project, the parking and turn around area located at the Cabrillo Mole approximately 120
  —

Pebbly Beach Road will be eliminated.
  —

To support taxi and tour operations, as well as traffic safety for all vehicles, City Staff propose:

  1. Installation of a temporary taxi line that will queue up on the paver walkway on Pebbly
  Beach Road, adjacent to the sea plane ramp. A temporary 8-foot-wide walkway will be
  constructed above the ramp adjacent to the payers to serve as the relocated walkway
  and loading area. The temporary taxi improvements include construction of a temporary
  deck, relocating the existing pedestrian guardrail, signing and striping.

  2. Installation of a vehicle turn around along Pebbly Beach Road, east of the Cabrillo Mole
  before Lover’s Cove. Improvements include installation/repositioning of k-rail, signage
  and striping to create a temporary vehicle turn around.

Pebbly Beach Road is frequently used by visitors, large commercial vehicles and residents and
is one of two roads that connects town to the industrial area.

Working cooperatively with W-Trans, California Traffic Engineering Consultants, City Staff
developed recommendations based on direction from the California Manual on Uniform Traffic
Control Devices (MUTCD) as well as engineering judgement, to make recommendations to
enhance the safety of the road.

City Staff is seeking approval of the plan by City Council before the installation of the
improvements. This is one of the requirements of a design immunity defense.

If approved, the proposed modifications will be installed in September 2026 and will remain in
place until the Cabrillo Mole Revitalization Project is completed.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Traffic safety.
 FISCAL IMPACTS: Undetermined.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING  RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  No  safety
improvements will be made to Wrigley Road.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

SUBJECT:  Contract for Stage 1 Design and Engineering Services Progressive
  Design-Build Contract for the Cabrillo Mole Revitalization Project
  Phase 2

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to finalize negotiations and
execute the Stage 1 design and engineering services progressive design-build contract for the
Cabrillo Mole Revitalization Phase 2 Project with Anderson Burton Construction, Inc. for a not-
to-exceed sum of $1.8 million.

REPORT SUMMARY: Public Contract Code § 22185 et seq. authorizes the City to use
progressive design-build contracting for the Progressive Design-Build Cabrillo Mole
Revitalization Phase 2 Project (“Project”).

At a high-level, this Project includes two stages: (1) preconstruction design phase services
(“Stage 1”); and (2) final design services and construction services to complete the Project
(“Stage 2”). The selected design-builder performs the Stage 1 design and engineering services
during or after which the design-builder proposes to City a Guaranteed Maximum Price
(‘GMP”) to construct the Project and, if accepted by City, the parties will enter into an
amendment to the contract for design-builder’s performance of Stage 2 services (final design
and construction). If the design is not acceptable to the City or the GMP too high, the City has
the option of not proceeding with Stage 2.

On May 19, 2026 the City Council authorized the City Manager to negotiate and bring back a
contract agreement with Anderson Burton Construction for City Council approval for the Stage
1 design and engineering services progressive design-build contract for the Cabrillo Mole
Revitalization Phase 2 Project.

After a series of meetings, City Staff and Anderson Burton representatives, including the
architect-of-record RRM Design Group, have successfully negotiated a base contract scope
  —

for Stage 1 of approximately $1.5 million.

Key Tasks included in this base contract scope include:
  • Project Commencement and Management
  o Project Initiation
  • Design Initiation
  o Document Review
   o Site Investigation & Existing Condition Verification
  o Conceptual Design
  •  Design Development
  o 100% Schematic Design
  o 100% design Development
  •  Construction Documents
  o 50% and 75% Construction Documents
  o Bidding and GMP Development

Not included in the base contract scope, but identified as potential additions to the Stage 1
contract, are the completion of 90% Construction Documents and the Final 100% Permitted
Construction Documents. City Staff and the Contractor opted to remove that scope of work
from the base bid so it can be delivered only if there is concurrence the final design is
accepted and the GMP will not exceed the City’s budget. This additional scope of work is
identified as an additional contract item with a value of approximately $200,000.

City Staff recommends the City Council authorize the City Manager to finalize negotiations and
execute the Stage 1 design and engineering services progressive design-build contract for the
Cabrillo Mole Revitalization Phase 2 Project with Anderson Burton Construction, Inc. for a not-
to-exceed sum of $1.8 million.

The not-to-exceed sum of $1.8 million will allow the City Manager the option to increase the
final scope to include completion of final construction documents as well as provide a small
contingency for additional contracted services.

City Staff anticipate a contract draft will be prepared for review legal and Los Angeles Metro
within the next week, and hope to issue a Notice to Proceed to Anderson Burton before June
30.

Stage 1 of this project is tentatively scheduled to take approximately 355 days. Construction
deliverables —  demolition of the current Cabrillo Mole Terminal, installation of temporary
facilities for the Cabrillo Mole Terminal tenants as well as procurement of long-lead items such
as the electrical switch board —  may be completed simultaneously to the Stage 1 scope of
work.

City Council will be provided regular updates on the design process as well as retain final
approval authority of the architectural design. After the design is approved, City Staff may
request authorization to negotiate and award an amendment with Anderson for the Stage 2
construction services.

FISCAL IMPACTS: This Project is budgeted in the FY 25-26 CIP Budget  —  Project # 180003-
1 and will utilize a combination of grant and general funding resources.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Infrastructure updates.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will not have
direction on how to proceed with the Cabrillo Mole Revitalization Project.
 FOLLOW UP ACTION: Begin negotiations with Anderson and bring back a final contract for
City Council consideration.

SUBJECT:  Proposed Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Continue discussing the proposed Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget.
If consensus, adopt the resolution establishing the City budget for Fiscal Year 2026-27.

REPORT SUMMARY: During the preceding three City Council meetings, Staff presented draft
versions of the proposed Fiscal Year 2026-27 operating and capital budgets as summarized
below:
  • April 19, 2026  —Discussion of beginning reserve estimates, year-to-date revenue
  estimates, projected revenues and preliminary operating budgets for the upcoming fiscal
  year
  • May 4, 2026 Discussion of operating budgets for çeneral Fund and Harbor Fund, as
  —

  well as proposed staffing levels
  • May 1 9, 2026 Discussion of operating budgets for Sewer, Saltwater, Solid Waste, and
  —

  Internal Service Funds

Copies of these presentations and draft budget are available on the Finance Department’s
webpage (https://www.cityofavalon.com/1 66/Budgets). Based on the input received during these
study sessions, Staff is presenting the proposed Fiscal Year 2026-27 Operating and Capital
Budget for City Council to review and consider for adoption. The proposed budget also includes
the City’s Budget and Fiscal Policies with no significant updates from the previously adopted
version.

The proposed budget includes expenditures totaling $69.84 million, including operating
expenditures of $38.23 million, capital outlays of $23.57 million, and internal service charges
and transfers of $8.03 million. The proposed budget represents a 10.9% increase from the
previous fiscal year.

The budget proposes increases in operating expenditures of $1 .22 million or 3.3%. Salaries and
benefits account for 33.9% of operating expenditures and are proposed to increase by $651
thousand or 5.3%. The increase is partially attributable to increases in unfunded pension liability
expenses of $131 thousand or 10.4%, in addition to wage and benefit increases as approved in
the memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with the City’s bargaining units adopted during the
current fiscal year. The proposed budget does not include any new full-time positions but
increases the number of budgeted part-time hours available for Recreation, Harbor Patrol, and
Public Works. While staffing levels remain below pre-pandemic levels, this approach reflects the
 City’s commitment to delivering a high-level of service both efficiently and sustainably.
Contracted services represent 49.3% of the operating budget and are budgeted to increase by
$419 thousand or 2.3%, with increases driven by inflation adjustment clauses in
contracts. Maintenance and operations account for the remaining 16.8% of operating
expenditures and are budgeted to increase by 3.1%. The overall modest increase in the
proposed operating budgets further demonstrates the City’s prudent use of public funds. The
increase in the proposed budget is driven by increases in capital outlays, with several major
capital projects scheduled for construction in the upcoming fiscal year.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Adopt a balanced City budget.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION:  City departments
would have to operate without the legal authority conveyed by adoption of the budget. The
Fiscal Year 2025-26 budget would continue to govern City expenditures.

FOLLOW UP ACTION:  Adopt the attached resolution establishing the budgets for all funds
and departments and approve the City’s Budget and Fiscal Policies.

 Introduction

Transmittal Letter
Honorable Mayor, Members of the City Council, and Community Members of the City of Avalon, California:

I am pleased to present the Proposed Fiscal Year 2026–27 Operating and Capital Budget for the City of Avalon. This
budget implements the direction provided by City Council and serves as the financial plan reflecting our shared
commitment to providing efficient public services and responsible investment in the City’s infrastructure in a
financially sustainable manner. The document has been prepared in accordance with state law, the Avalon Municipal
Code, and the City Council’s adopted financial policies.

The proposed budget includes expenditures totaling $69.84 million, including operating expenditures of $38.23
million, capital outlays of $23.57 million, and internal service charges and transfers of $8.03 million. The proposed
budget represents a 10.9% increase from the previous fiscal year.

The budget proposes increases in operating expenditures of $1.22 million or 3.3%. Salaries and benefits account for
33.9% of operating expenditures and are proposed to increase by $651 thousand or 5.3%. The increase is partially
attributable to increases in unfunded pension liability expenses of $131 thousand or 10.4%, in addition to wage and
benefit increases as approved in the memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with the City's bargaining units
adopted during the current fiscal year. The proposed budget does not include any new full-time positions but
increases the number of budgeted part-time hours available for Recreation, Harbor Patrol, and Public Works. While
staffing levels remain below pre-pandemic levels, this approach reflects the City's commitment to delivering a high-
level of service both efficiently and sustainably. Contracted services represent 49.3% of the operating budget and are
budgeted to increase by $419 thousand or 2.3%, with increases driven by inflation adjustment clauses in contracts.
 Maintenance and operations account for the remaining 16.8% of operating expenditures and are budgeted to increase
by 3.1%. The overall modest increase in the proposed operating budgets further demonstrates the City's prudent use of
public funds.

While carefully managing operating costs, the City has been successful in obtaining grant funding, while leveraging
existing reserves from increases in wharfage rates adopted over the last fiscal year, to fund several vital infrastructure
projects in the harbor scheduled for construction during the upcoming fiscal year. The City anticipates construction of
a 100-foot groin wall and repairs to the seawall to begin at South Beach during the fall, with sand replenishment to
restore the beach in time for the next summer season. The funds provided in prior capital budgets for design and
engineering enabled the City to successfully obtain $2.48 million in funding from the Los Angeles County Regional
Park and Open Space District (RPOSD) Measure A Grant, accelerating the City's ability to bring South Beach back to
the community and visitors alike. During the fall, the City also anticipates replacing the decking and existing electrical
infrastructure on the Green Pleasure Pier, with $1.00 million in state funding provided by State Senator Lena Gonzales
to assist with this project. Additional grant-funded projects in the Harbor, scheduled for construction in the fall,
include the Clubdock Dinghy Dock Pier Replacement and End Float Replacement, with grant funding from the
California Department of Boating and Waterways Boating Infrastructure Grant (BIG) program. Given the extended
summer season and challenges with construction during the winter months, the fall will be a critical period with
significant construction around the harbor. While there may be temporary disruptions, the resulting improvements
will provide lasting value to the community for decades to come.

During the current fiscal year, the City issued a request for proposals for the design-build of the Cabrillo Mole Ferry
Terminal and anticipates awarding the contract to begin the formal design phase in the coming weeks. This milestone
marks nearly a decade of planning by the City, including the completion of significant substructure repairs to the
concrete decking, steel grating, riprap and pilings. The City anticipates the design phase to cover approximately nine
months, with construction anticipated to start during the fourth quarter of the upcoming fiscal year. During the first

In addition to these harbor projects, the City remains focused on critical infrastructure needs throughout the City. The

Budget Overview
Each year, the City Council adopts, by formal resolution, an annual budget. This document serves as a financial plan,
identifying the projected allocation and application of resources over the budget cycle. The published Operating and
Capital Budget is designed to present summary information about the City’s financial plans for the year in a user-
friendly format. The budget is organized by fund and department. Expenditures are displayed and subtotaled by the
following types: Salaries & Benefits; Maintenance & Operations; Contract Services; and Capital Outlays.

Line-item budget development is accomplished through the City’s online budget building tool, which allows each
department to build its operating budget using computerized worksheets. The individual departments are directly
responsible for developing the Maintenance & Operations and Contract Services expenditure budgets. Salary & Benefit
information is calculated and entered by the Finance Department based on salary schedules and applicable
memorandums of understanding (MOU). New budget requests (e.g. new personnel, services, equipment) are
identified by the Finance Director and presented separately for the City Manager’s review and approval before
becoming part of the proposed operating budget. The Finance Director also provides the City Manager with revenue
projections. These projections are reviewed with the department budget requests to determine available funding
levels for the upcoming fiscal year. The City Manager and Finance Director then hold meetings with the departments
to review the operating budgets and additional budget requests. Once the budget data has been reviewed and any
changes have been made by the Finance Department, a proposed budget document is prepared. After review and
approval by the City Manager, the proposed budget document is presented to City Council, with at least one study
session and public presentation, prior to adoption. During the fiscal year, the budget can be amended as necessary by
City Council to meet the City’s needs. The City’s budget and fiscal policies outline internal controls for transfers within
budgeted accounts.

Basis of Accounting
The City budget is maintained using the modified accrual basis of accounting, which recognizes expenditures when
the related fund liability is incurred. Revenues are recognized when they become both they become measurable and
available. Measurable means the amount of the transaction can be determined and available means collectible within
the current period or soon enough thereafter to be used to pay liabilities of the current period. For budget
presentation purposes, the City records capital outlays as an expense to assist with budgetary control. At year-end, the
amounts are converted to capital assets, as appropriate, for presentation in audited financial statements. The City’s
governmental funds are also reported on a modified accrual basis of accounting in the City’s Annual Comprehensive
Financial Report (ACFR) fund statements; however, the Enterprise and Internal Service Funds are reported on a full
accrual basis in the ACFR.

The City’s accounting system is maintained on a fund basis, in accordance with governmental accounting standards.
Each of the City’s funds is considered a separate accounting entity with a self-balancing set of accounts that record
assets, liabilities, fund equity, revenues and expenditures. Funds are established and segregated for the purpose of
recording specific programs or attaining certain objectives in accordance with special regulations restrictions, or
limitations. Funds are classified into one of three categories: governmental (general fund, special revenues),
proprietary (enterprise and internal service), and fiduciary (trust or agency). Governmental funds account for activities
generally associated with local government operations. Proprietary funds are financed and operated in a manner
similar to private business enterprises, where the intent is to recover the costs of providing goods and services from
users through charges for services. Fiduciary funds are utilized in situations where the government is acting in a
fiduciary capacity as a trustee.

The operating budget document includes citywide information as well as information specific to each fund and each
department. The City receives revenue from numerous sources, many of which have restrictions on how funds can be
used. Separate funds are established to account for the different types of revenues and their allowable uses. The
following Classification of Funds describes, in detail, the various types of funds and their purpose as established by the
City of Avalon.
