Types of Funds
GOVERNMENTAL FUND TYPES

General Fund is used to account for resources traditionally associated with general government which are not
required to be accounted for in a separate fund, including: sales tax, property tax, transient occupancy tax, licenses and
permits, fines and forfeitures. In general, these funds are allocated at the discretion of the City Council. This revenue is
used to support citywide services such as public safety, community services, planning, and public works. Other non-
major funds are aggregated with General Fund activity for budget presentation purposes.

Special Revenue Funds are used to account for the proceeds of revenues that are designated for specific or restricted
uses. These funds include gas tax funds from the State, sales tax funds from the County dedicated for public
transportation, and Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds from the federal government. The Street
Administration Fund is used to account for the City’s share of State and County gasoline tax collection in accordance
with the provisions of the State of California Streets and Highway Code. Revenues are disbursed by the State based on
population and must be used towards the maintenance and repair of City streets. The Traffic Safety Fund is used to
account for fines collected and are used to fund eligible traffic safety and code enforcement expenditures.
Expenditures in excess of fines collected are covered through budgeted transfers from the General Fund. The
Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Fund is used to account for the receipts and expenditures of CDBG
funds received from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. The Local Transportation Fund is used
to account for the proceeds from Proposition A and C and Measures R and M, additional sales tax generated by the
approval of Los Angeles County voters administered by the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA)
for transportation-related projects, collectively referred to as Local Return funds. These funds are used to support the
cross-channel commuter subsidy program and local public transportation, including fixed-route and dial-a-ride
services. The Avalon Housing Authority Fund is used to account for activity associated with the City’s continued
housing operations. This fund was created effective February 1, 2012 as a result of legislation enacted by the State of
California.

PROPRIETARY FUND TYPES

Enterprise Funds are established to function as self-supporting operations wherein expenditures are entirely offset by
fees or charges for services. Revenues from fees or charges are accounted for in separate enterprise funds and can
only be used to pay for expenses related to those services. The Harbor Fund is used to account for all harbor
operations, including the fuel dock. The Sewer Fund was established to receive and disburse funds collected through
sewer service charge fees and sewer facilities charges. This fund is used for the operation and maintenance of sewer
disposal facilities and the financing of construction for sewer outlets. The Saltwater Fund was established to receive
charges for the operation of the City’s saltwater pumping plants and systems. The Solid Waste Fund was established to
account for solid waste collection and disposal costs. The Avalon Transit Fund was established to account for the
portion of the City’s local public transportation operations not covered by the Local Transportation Fund.

Internal Service Funds are established to account for a variety of business services provided by one City department
(or division) to other City departments. Departments are charged for these services based on their respective
utilization. The General Administration Fund is used to account for general administration costs, including the City
Manager’s office, finance, information technology, legal, provided to other funds and departments on a cost
reimbursement basis. The Insurance Fund is used to account for the City’s general liability program. The Vehicle
Maintenance Fund is used to account for the operation, maintenance, and replacement of City vehicles. Revenues are
generated from each department’s share of operating costs.

FIDUCIARY FUND TYPES

Private Purpose Trust Fund accounts for various assets held in trust for other governments, individuals, or the public
at large. The funds are custodial in nature and do not involve measurement of results of operations. The Successor

 Community Profile

Community Profile
The City of Avalon is the only incorporated community located on Santa Catalina Island, approximately twenty-two
miles off the coast of Southern California. The City is situated on the leeward side of the island around Avalon Bay, and
its jurisdictional boundaries occupy just under three square miles or less than five percent (5%) of the entire island. The
City serves a population of approximately 3,400 residents and welcomes over one million visitors each year through its
picturesque harbor, with most residents and visitors arriving through the City’s Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal.

The City of Avalon is located entirely within the coastal zone, and the local economy is centered on tourism. As most of
the City is already built-out, new development primarily comes from infill which helps to preserve the compact,
walkable character of the City. The autoette, which is smaller and travels at lower speeds compared to traditional
automobiles, is the most common method of transportation in the City and the City closely regulates both the size
and number of vehicles permitted to facilitate congestion and encourage active transportation. The City’s Green
Pleasure Pier serves as the hub for commercial and recreational ocean-based activities, including fishing, scuba diving,
parasailing and kayaking. In addition to the natural open space areas, the City offers multiple parks, picnic areas, and
public beaches for both residents and visitors to enjoy.

Incorporated on June 26, 1913, as a general law city, the City operates under the Council-Manager form of government
with a five-member City Council elected by the citizens of Avalon. The Mayor is directly elected to serve a two-year
term and Council Members are elected at large to alternating four-year terms. The City Council serves as the policy-
making body of the City; adopting the budget, enacting local ordinances, appointing committees, and directing such
actions as required to provide for the general welfare of the community. The City Manager, appointed by the City
Council, is responsible for the administration of all City affairs and the implementation of all policies and ordinances
established by the City Council. The City Attorney serves under contract and is appointed by the City Council. All other
staff are appointed by the City Manager.

History of the City
Prior to colonization, the area around Avalon Bay was inhabited for thousands of years by the Tongva (Gabrielino) tribe,
who called the island Pimu or Pimugna. The Tongva had settlements all over the island, including in present-day
Avalon. They were renowned for their mining and working with soapstone found on the island, and traveled frequently
to the mainland for trade.

The first European to record seeing the island was Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo in 1542 during a Spanish expedition.
Another Spanish explorer, Sebastian Vizcaino, arrived at the island on the eve of Saint Catherine's Day (November 24)
of 1602 and named the island in the saint's honor. The island was used for ranching, mining, whaling, and otter
hunting up until the end of the 19th century.

In 1887, real estate developer George Shatto purchased Catalina Island from the estate of James Lick with the vision of
turning it into a coastal resort. Shatto named the settlement Avalon, after the mystical isle of Avalon from Arthurian
legend as featured in Lord Tennyson's poem Idylls of the King. He built the first pier and the first hotel and mapped
out the streets used to this day. While establishing tourism in Avalon, Shatto defaulted on his loan and the island
returned to the Lick estate. The sons of Phinneas Banning bought the island in 1891 and established the Santa Catalina
Island Company to further develop it as a resort. The City of Avalon was incorporated during this period and purchased
the Green Pleasure Pier from the Santa Catalina Island Company in 1914.

In 1919, William Wrigley Jr. bought a controlling interest in the Santa Catalina Island Company and invested heavily in
infrastructure and tourism, including the construction of the Catalina Casino in 1929. As a result, Avalon became a
popular filming location and favorite retreat for Hollywood stars. During World War II, the island was closed to tourism
and was repurposed for military training. After the war, the City reopened to tourism and, in 1968, the City constructed

welcoming cruise ship visitors to the City. Today, the City welcomes over one million visitors annually through its

 General Fund

General Fund
The General Fund is the main operating fund for the City. It accounts for sources and uses of resources that primarily
are discretionary to the City Council in the provision of activities, programs, and services deemed necessary and
desirable by the community. The major revenue sources for this fund are transient occupancy tax (TOT), sales tax,
admission tax, property tax, licenses, charges for services, permits and fees. Expenditures are made for public safety
(including law enforcement and fire), public works, planning, and other community services.

structurally balanced budget, with reserves being utilized to cover one-time capital outlays.

Visitor-driven tax revenues make up the majority of General Fund revenues. As highlighted in this chart, the City has
historically adopted a conservative approach to revenue estimates for visitor-driven tax revenues and fees, due to its
reliance on tourism demand. Visitor-driven revenues fluctuate year-to-year based on external economic conditions
and this approach has allowed the City to operate in a sustainable manner, building reserves when actual revenues
exceed budget estimates.

Visitor-driven tax revenues, including Transient Occupancy Tax (TOT), Sales Tax, and Admission Tax, account for
approximately 70% of revenues in the General Fund.

TOT is estimated at $7,725,000 for the next fiscal year. This represents a decrease of $475,500 or 5.8% from the
estimated revenues in the current year. The City has historically budgeted TOT revenues below current year actuals to
not require record-setting overnight visitor levels to balance the budget. Taxes remitted by hotels account for
approximately 67% of total TOT collections with approximately 33% remitted by short-term vacation rental
properties. The City remits 22% of the TOT collected to the Love Catalina Island Tourism Authority to fund marketing
and promotion activities.

Sales tax revenues are estimated to be flat compared to the current year based on forecasts prepared by the City's
sales tax consultant. One percent of the current 10.25% sales and use tax rate in the City, commonly referred to as the
Bradley-Burns Local Tax, is distributed to the City’s General Fund. Restaurants account for more than half of taxable
sales activity in the City.

Similar to TOT, Admission Tax revenues of $881,500 are budgeted to be down 7.3% or $69,500 from current year
estimates. Admission tax is a 4% tax on gross receipts for all ticketed tours, activities, and events in the City.

 Fire Department

Fire Department
The City's Fire Department consists of the Fire Chief, three Fire Captains, three Fire Engineers, and three Firefighters.
In addition, the City added a part-time administrative assistant position in the FY2026 Budget. The City also maintains
a force of up to thirty (30) volunteer firefighters.

Salaries and benefits account for 66.7% of department expenditures and budgeted amounts are based on negotiated
wages and benefits included in memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with the IAFF and Management bargaining
units. The decrease in salaries and benefits was driven by changes to how the City allocates unfunded pension
liabilities for Safety members between the Harbor and Fire Department, resulting in a savings to the Fire Department
budget of $118 thousand.

Internal Service Fund expenditures account for 17.0% of department expenditures. The Fire Department is charged
10.7% of General Administration Fund expenditures, 12.1% of Insurance Fund expenditures, and 10.5% of Vehicle
Maintenance Fund expenditures. The decrease in budgeted expenditures from the prior year is attributable to
changes in the allocation amount for the Vehicle Maintenance Fund. The Fire Department's share of fund
expenditures was reduced from 17.5%, as recent vehicle and equipment acquisitions have been charged directly to its
budget and the significant capital outlays in the Vehicle Maintenance Fund over recent years have primarily benefited
other departments.

Capital outlays account for 10.2% of budgeted expenditures and include funding for Fire Command 1, fire station
improvements, and a grant-funded purchase of an electric stretcher.

Maintenance and operations account for 6.1% of department expenditures. Expenditures relate to ambulance supplies,
equipment, communications, fuel, uniforms, and training and travel. The decrease from the current fiscal year is
attributable to one-time grant funded expenditures in the current year.

 Other General Fund Activity

Other General Fund Activity
Other General Fund expenditures relate to the Storm Drain Fund, Successor Agency Administration, and internal
service allocations and transfers assigned to the General Fund.

The City charges a portion of the contract for managing the wastewater treatment plant (approximately 5%) to the
Storm Drain Fund, which is funded through transfers by the General Fund. The General Fund also subsidizes the Traffic
Safety Fund, Street Administration, and Avalon Transit Funds through transfers, as citations, gasoline taxes, and Local
Return funds are not sufficient to fully fund these operations. In addition to transfers, the General Fund assumes the
share of internal service charges for Special Revenue Funds, including the Housing Authority, Local Transportation,
Traffic Safety, and Street Administration, to comply with specific requirements in these funds and to ensure the other
Enterprise Funds are not charged a disproportionate amount for the services they receive. These charges account for
16.3% of General Administration Fund and 18.5% of Insurance Fund expenditures.

Lastly, the City receives an administrative allowance for managing the Successor Agency. A portion of the Finance
Director's time (10%) is charged to the fund for managing the reporting process, along with contracted services with
RSG Solutions, who assist with County and State reporting requirements. The decrease in budgeted allowance and
associated expenditures is the result of decreased activity to be reported.

Housing Authority
The Housing Authority’s primary activities are maintaining the former Avalon Community Improvement Agency's
assets, such as properties and affordability agreements, including the 206 East Whittley Avenue property.

Capital outlays include construction for the 206 East Whittley Retaining Wall Remediation Project. In developing the
plan for a potential second building, geotechnical engineers determined the existing retaining walls at the property’s
boundaries need remediation to extend their service life due to corrosion on the existing tiebacks and age of the
concrete. Other capital projects include the preliminary design and engineering of additional low-moderate income
housing developments within the City limits.

Contract services include the City's contract with RSG Solutions, who assist City Staff with reporting and other
compliance requirements, and the City Attorney. In addition, the City charges a portion of the City Manager's time to
the Housing Authority. Previously, the City also charged a portion of the Assistant City Manager and Public Works
Director to the fund for their involvement in managing housing-related activities.

 Local Transportation

Local Transportation
The Local Transportation Fund accounts for transit-related activity in the City of Avalon, including the City of Avalon
Seaside Transit (COAST) point-to-point shuttle service and cross-channel commuter subsidy program, which are
funded utilizing various intergovernmental revenues including Local Return funds and Transportation Development
Act Article 3 and Article 8 (TDA) funds.

Local Return Funds refer to four one-half cent sales tax measures approved by Los Angeles County voters to finance
countywide transit development programs, which include Proposition A, Proposition C, Measure M, and Measure R
funds. In addition to these funds, which are distributed on a per-capita basis by the Los Angeles Metropolitan
Transportation Authority (METRO), the City annually applies for and receives Proposition A Discretionary funds, which
are used primarily to fund the commuter subsidy program, as well as to offset costs associated with COAST. TDA funds
are state funds derived from a quarter cent sales tax and from sales tax on diesel fuel.

 Nonmajor (Special Revenue) Funds

Nonmajor (Special Revenue) Funds
Special Revenue Funds are used to account for the proceeds of revenues that are designated for specific or restricted
uses. In addition to the Housting Authority and Local Transportation Funds, the City uses special revenue funds for
Traffic Safety, Street Administration, Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), and the Mclean Putnam Hall
Funds. The City also has separate funds for the five development impact fees. These funds are classified as nonmajor
funds based on their size relative to the City's other major funds.

The Traffic Safety Fund is used to account for citation revenues which are restricted to be used for parking
enforcement, traffic control and other code enforcement activities.

The Street Administration Fund is used to account for various gasoline tax revenues received by the City which are
restricted to be used for street maintenance and related improvements.

The CDBG Fund is used to account for grant revenues received through a federal grant program to help communities
develop urban areas. The City receives an annual allocation of less than $40 thousand through this program. Over the
last several years, the City has used these funds to enhance the ADA-accessibility of streets and sidewalks through
curb cuts and other improvements. Given the relatively small amount received, the City rolls over funds for several
years until enough has accumulated to efficiently fund an ADA-related project. The City does not have any proposed
budgeted activity in this fund for the current year.

The Mclean Putnam Hall Fund was established to account for donations to the Fire Department for the purchase of
fire-related equipment. The City does not have any proposed budgeted activity in this fund for the current year but will
request amendments to the budget as projects are identified or as additional funds become available.

 Street Administration

Street Administration
The Street Administration Fund is used to track expenditures of funds received from the City's share of state gasoline
taxes in accordance with the provisions of the State of California Streets and Highway Code.

The City receives Highway Users Tax Account (HUTA) funding under Sections 2103, 2105, 2106, 2107, and 2107.5 and Road
Maintenance and Rehabilitation Account (RMRA) funding under Section 2032. The City has historically used HUTA
funding to provide contracted street sweeping services and funding for annual road maintenance. The City has used
RMRA funding as part of its local match for the Five Corner's Pedestrian Improvement Project.

The proposed budget includes additional funding for an assessment of current road conditions to be performed prior
to the Citywide Street Paving Project. This project will be primarily funded by a transfer from the General Fund.

 Traffic Safety

Traffic Safety
The Traffic Safety Fund is used to account for citation revenues resulting from violations of the California Vehicle Code,
which are restricted to being used for parking enforcement, traffic control and other code enforcement activities.
Annual citation revenues are not sufficient to fund current enforcement activities and the fund is subsidized annually
through a transfer from the General Fund.

Salaries and benefits, based on negotiated MOUs, account for 80.3% of expenditures in this fund. Budgeted positions
include a Lead Code Enforcement Officer, a Code Enforcement Officer, and two (2) vacant part-time Parking
Enforcement Officer positions. Contract services account for 10.9% of budgeted expenditures and include $25,000 for
contracted Vehicle Hearing Officer services and $25,000 for contracted Animal Control services, an increase of $15,000
from the prior year's budget.

self-sustaining manner.

 Harbor Operations

Harbor Operations
Within the Harbor Fund, the City tracks operating activities of the harbor separately from capital activities and the fuel
dock. Operating activities include Harbor Administration, Harbor Operations, including Harbor Patrol and Harbor
Sanitation activities, and Public Works operations along the waterfront.

Harbor Operations are primarily funded by charges for services, including a portion of cross-channel and cruise ship
wharfage dedicated to operations and nightly mooring revenues. Similar to other visitor-driven revenues in the
General Fund, harbor operating revenues are budgeted conservatively below current year actuals for cross-channel
wharfage and nightly moorings to ensure operations are fully funded without requiring record-setting levels of
tourism year-after-year. Cruise ship wharfage revenues are estimated based on arriving vessels scheduled as of April
30th, assuming an 87% occupancy rate, compared to 92% occupancy rate experienced in the current year to date.

Harbor Administration accounts for 9.8% of budgeted expenditures. Harbor Operations, including Harbor Patrol,
accounts for 56.2% of budgeted expenditures and Public Works accounts for the remaining 34.0% of budgeted
expenditures. A breakdown of expenditures by type (e.g. Salaries and Benefits, Maintenance and Operations, Contract
Services, and Internal Services) can be found in the next section of the budget document.

 Salaries and Benefits Fund 103

Salaries and Benefits
Budgeted amounts for salaries and benefits are based on negotiated wages and benefits as outlined in MOUs with the
applicable bargaining units and CalPERS unfunded pension liability payment schedules and represent 44.2% of
Harbor Operations budgeted expenditures. Salaries and benefits within Harbor Operations include the following
personnel:

  Harbor Administration (1.90 FTE): Senior Harbor Operations Assistant (1.00), Harbor Master (0.90)
  Harbor Operations (17.22): Harbor Patrol Supervisors (2.00), Harbor Patrol Officers - Full-Time (9.00), Harbor Patrol
  Officers - PT (4.62), Harbor Sanitation Workers (1.60)
  Harbor Public Works (5.75): Public Works Director (0.30), Project Manager (0.4), Maintenance Superintendents
  (0.50), Maintenance Lead Worker (0.25), Maintenance Workers - Full-TIme (3.60), Maintenance Workers - Part-
  Time (0.70)

Harbor Maintenance Workers (3.00 FTE) were included with Harbor Operations in prior budgets but have been
reclassified to Harbor Capital as their job duties more accurately align with capital maintenance of the harbor.

Despite the reallocation of Harbor Maintenance personnel, Harbor Operations Salaries and Benefits increased by 13.6%,
driven by increases in unfunded pension liability payments of $231,758, representing an 84.4% increase from the prior
year liability payment. Previously, the City allocated pension liabilities between Classic and PEPRA membership
separately, based on a weighted average of salary in each classification. Over time, as Classic employees retired, this
approach skewed the costs to the Safety department with the most current Classic members rather than historical
membership distributions representative of the liability as incurred. To correct this issue, Classic and PEPRA members
in the Harbor Department and Fire Department were combined with unfunded pension liability allocated based on
the weighted average of salary in each department rather than based on membership classification.

 Harbor Capital

Harbor Capital
Harbor Capital reflects annual maintenance activities of harbor infrastructure, including floats, piers, ramps, and
moorings, as well as new capital acquisitions and significant refurbishments of existing assets intended to extend their
useful life.

During the prior fiscal year, the City increased the per passenger cross-channel and cruise ship wharfage fees to
generate revenues sufficient to fund significant investments needed in the harbor. Cross-channel and cruise ship
wharfage increases went into effect in September 2025 and January 2026, respectively. As the result of a full year with
these increases, Harbor Capital charges for service are budgeted to increase by $869 thousand or 21.1% from the prior
year. Grants and Intergovernmental Revenues represent the other sources of Harbor Capital revenues, with revenues
received as reimbursements for actual expenditures incurred. During the current fiscal year, the City successfully
obtained grant funding for several critical infrastructure projects, including $2.48 million for the South Beach
Restoration Project, $1.00 million for the Green Pleasure Pier Decking Replacement Project, and $300 thousand for
replacement of the Pier End Float. In addition, the City anticipates awarding the design-build contract for the Cabrillo
Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation Project, with construction anticipated to start during the second half of the
upcoming fiscal year.

While Capital Outlays account for 90.8% of budgeted expenditures, the City also budgets capital maintenance
activities for Harbor Capital. Salaries and benefits, totaling $346 thousand, represent 2.4% of the Harbor Capital
budget. Salaries and benefits include two full-time Harbor Maintenance Workers, one Maintenance Lead Worker, and
a portion of the Harbor Master's labor costs (0.10 FTE). Harbor Maintenance Workers were budgeted with Harbor
Operations in previous budgets but were reassigned to Harbor Capital to better align the labor allocation to the
positions' responsibilities. Maintenance and Operations expenditures, totaling $374 thousand, represent an additional
2.4% of Harbor Capital budgeted expenditures. Internal Service expenditures totaling $629 thousand represent 4.1% of
budgeted expenditures for Harbor Capital, which represent 9.6% of General Administration expenditures and 22.0% of
Vehicle Maintenance expenditures.

 Sewer Fund

Sewer Fund
The Sewer Fund is used to account for the operation and maintenance of the collection and distribution system and
the waste water treatment plant (WWTP).

As an enterprise fund, the Sewer Fund is funded through service charges to users of the sewer system. Sewer service
rates are determined based on the findings of a cost of service study pursuant to Proposition 218 requirements. Sewer
revenues are budgeted to increase by 9.5% in the upcoming fiscal year to provide additional funding for significant
capital investment. Sewer service charges are assessed on parcels through the property tax roll by the County of Los
Angeles.

Contract services account for 45.5% of budgeted expenditures. The City contracts with PERC Water Corporation for the
operation of the WWTP, which accounts for 90.1% of contract service expenditures and 41.0% of total fund
expenditures. The City allocates 75% of the PERC contract to the Sewer Fund, with the remaining 25% charged to the
Saltwater and Storm Drain Funds. Other contract services include Fats, Oil Grease (FOG) inspection services, falconry
services, and various testing and permitting services. Capital outlays account for 23.6% of budgeted expenditures and
are outlined in the Capital Improvement Plan section of the budget document. Maintenance and operations account
for 12.3% of budgeted expenditures. Utilities at the wastewater treatment plant and pump stations account for over
half of all maintenance and operations expenditures. Internal service charges account for 11.6% of budgeted
expenditures, with the Sewer Fund responsible for 6.5% of the General Administration Fund, 8.6% of the Insurance
Fund, and 13.5% of the Vehicle Maintenance Fund. Lastly, salaries and benefits account for 7.0% of budgeted
expenditures, with 1.75 FTEs from Public Works and 0.20 FTEs from Code Enforcement charged to the fund.

 Saltwater Fund

Saltwater Fund
The Saltwater Fund is used to account for the operation and maintenance of the collection and distribution system
related to saltwater service.

As an enterprise fund, the Saltwater Fund is funded through service charges to users of the sewer system. Saltwater
service rates are determined based on the findings of a cost of service study pursuant to Proposition 218 requirements.
Saltwater revenues are budgeted to increase by 9.5% in the upcoming fiscal year to provide additional funding for
significant capital investment. Saltwater service charges are assessed on parcels through the property tax roll by the
County of Los Angeles.

Contract services account for 40.9% of budgeted expenditures. The City contracts with PERC Water Corporation for the
operation of the WWTP, which accounts for 98.7% of contract service expenditures and 40.4% of total fund
expenditures. The City allocates 20% of the PERC contract to the Sewer Fund, with the remaining 80% charged to the
Sewer and Storm Drain Funds. Capital outlays account for 31.4% of budgeted expenditures and are outlined in the
Capital Improvement Plan section of the budget document. Salaries and benefits account for 17.4% of budgeted
expenditures, with 1.25 FTEs from Public Works charged to the fund. Internal service charges account for 9.7% of
budgeted expenditures, with the Saltwater Fund responsible for 2.2% of the General Administration Fund and 2.4% of
the Insurance Fund. Lastly, maintenance and operation expenditures account for the remaining 0.7% of budgeted
expenditures.

 Solid Waste Fund

Solid Waste Fund
The Solid Waste Fund is used to account for waste collection operations and the management of the City-owned,
Pebbly Beach Landfill.

As an enterprise fund, the Solid Waste Fund is funded through service charges to users of the waste collection service
and landfill. Solid waste service rates are determined based on the findings of a cost of service study pursuant to
Proposition 218 requirements. Solid Waste revenues are budgeted to increase by 2.0% in the upcoming fiscal year.
Solid waste service charges are assessed on parcels through the property tax roll by the County of Los Angeles.

Contract services account for 65.7% of budgeted expenditures. The City contracts with CR&R Environmental Services
for waste collection and landfill operation services, which accounts for 90.6% of contract service expenditures and
59.5% of total fund expenditures. Other contract services include hazardous waste collection and disposal services.
Capital outlays account for 27.0% of budgeted expenditures and include permitting and engineering for the landfill
expansion, as well as the replacement of the landfill's grinder/chipper. Internal service charges account for 5.9% of
budgeted expenditures, with the Solid Waste Fund responsible for 4.2% of the General Administration Fund and 4.8%
of the Insurance Fund. Salaries and benefits account for 0.8% of budgeted expenditures, with 0.20 FTEs from Code
Enforcement charged to the fund for management of the green waste inspection program. Lastly, maintenance and
operations account for 0.7% of budgeted expenditures, with the majority in this category related to rent at disposal
locations.

 Avalon Transit

Avalon Transit
The Avalon Transit Fund is used to account for the City's land transit program expenditures to the extent that they are
not covered by Local Return and TDA funds, as recorded in the Local Transportation Fund. The City of Avalon operates
an all-electric, app-based, point-to-point, micro-transit system called City of Avalon Seaside Transit (COAST) through its
contract with Circuit, Inc.

As an enterprise fund, the Avalon Transit Fund is funded through fare-box revenues. The transit program in Avalon has
also historically been subsidized through transfers from the General Fund, as fare-box revenues and Local Return
funds are not sufficient to cover the cost of operations. Contract services account for 36.8% of budgeted expenditures.
The contract services amount represents an estimate of the City's contract with Circuit that is not covered by Local
Return or TDA funds. Internal service charges account for 27.2% of budgeted expenditures, with the Avalon Transit
Fund responsible for 1.4% of the General Administration Fund and 3.0% of the Vehicle Maintenance Fund. The Avalon
Transit Fund is not assessed for costs associated with the Insurance Fund as transit activities are covered under a
separate policy reflected in the maintenance and operations expenditure category. Maintenance and operations
account for 23.7% of budgeted expenditures and also include vehicle maintenance costs performed by third-parties.
Lastly, salaries and benefits account for 12.4% of budgeted expenditures and include a portion of an Administrative
Analyst's labor cost (0.25 FTE).

 Internal Service Funds

Internal Service Funds
The City utilizes internal service funds to track costs for goods and services incurred internally in support of other
funds or departments and then allocates those costs to the funds receiving the goods and services based on the
amount of benefit received. Internal service funds include the General Administration Fund, Insurance Fund, and
Vehicle Maintenance Fund.

Internal Service Allocations
Annually, during the budget development process, the Finance Department evaluates the allocation of internal
service costs across funds and departments to ensure allocations are proportional to the amount of service received.

General Administration allocations are based on the average of expenditure amounts, expenditure volume, and FTE
counts relative to each department and fund. Special revenue funds, including Local Transportation, Housing
Authority, Street Administration, and Traffic Safety, are not assessed any internal service charges with their
proportional share covered by the General Fund.

Insurance Fund allocations are based on similar criteria to General Administration, with departments which acquire
separate insurance policies (e.g. Law Enforcement, which is included in the services contract with the Los Angeles
County Sheriff's Department, Harbor Capital and Avalon Transit) excluded from the allocation. In addition, the amount
allocated to funds is increased based on funds or departments with historical experience of significant claims (e.g.
Harbor Operations, and Sewer Fund).

Vehicle Maintenance Funds are allocated based on estimates of time spent by City mechanics and a review of actual
expenditures. For the current fiscal year, the Fire Department's share was reduced. This reduction was made in
consideration that the recent significant capital outlays in the Vehicle Maintenance Fund did not directly serve the
Fire Department and recent vehicle acquisitions for the Fire Department have been charged directly to the Fire
Department budget rather than through the Vehicle Maintenance Fund.

 General Administration

General Administration
The General Administration Fund is used to account for expenditures related to elected officials, general services
performed by the City Attorney, the City Manager's Office, City Clerk, Human Resources, Information Technology (IT)
and Finance, as well as to account for retiree health insurance reimbursements and general maintenance and supplies
for City Hall.

Administration, which includes the City Manager's Office, City Clerk, Human Resources, and IT, accounts for 46.6% of
budgeted expenditures in the fund. General Government accounts for 24.4% of budgeted expenditures in the fund
and includes utilities, maintenance of City Hall, retiree health insurance reimbursements, and contracted services with
Townsend Consulting and external auditors. Finance accounts for 22.8% of budgeted expenditures and includes
financial reporting and budgeting software in addition to department personnel. City Attorney and Elected Officials
account for the remaining 6.2% of budgeted expenditures.

Salaries and benefits account for 69.5% of budgeted expenditures across all departments, increasing by 11.6% from the
prior year's budget. A portion of the increase is attributable to changes in employee allocations, with portions of the
City Manager and Assistant City Manager costs shifting from Housing Authority to the General Administration Fund.
The proposed budget also includes an increase in part-time hours available for the Administrative Assistant position.

 Hospital Fund

Hospital Fund
The City collects two different tax measures on behalf of Catalina Island Health (CIH).

Avalon's Measure C is a half-cent add-on sales tax which passed by the voters in Avalon in April 2000 and generates
approximately $800 thousand annually to fund hospital and clinic operations. The City receives these funds on a
monthly basis from the state and remits the amounts received directly to the hospital.

Avalon's Measure H is a special tax on all individuals arriving in Avalon, via cross-channel carriers, cruise ships, aircraft,
or private boat, to finance the construction of a new hospital facility. The revenues generated by this tax are deposited
into a separate account and the City reimburses CIH for eligible expenditures incurred. As of April 30, 2026, the City has
reimbursed CIH for $3.6 million in expenditures related to design, permitting, and engineering.

The fund balance is reported as a restricted balance within the General Fund in audited financial statements.

 Capital Improvement Plan

Capital Improvement Plan
The Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) is a strategic roadmap that outlines the City's commitment to enhancing our
community's infrastructure and assets. This document serves as a comprehensive guide to long-term investment
strategies, highlighting goals, projects, funding strategies, and implementation timelines.

Capital Budgeting Process
The Capital Budget (the first year) and Improvement Plan (the following four years) are a forecast of the City's
infrastructure needs and a plan for funding and implementing those capital projects. Unlike the City's operating
budget, capital projects can be funded over multiple years and appropriations can be carried forward from year to
year. Funds in the first year are appropriated by the City Council, while future years represent planned expenditures
that have not yet been authorized.

Definitions and Criteria for Capital Projects
In general, capital projects are activities related to the acquisition, construction, and long-term investment in publicly
owned capital assets. Long-term investment means funding for renovations or significant repairs but not routine
maintenance. Capital assets include land, building and related improvements (e.g new roof on City Hall),
improvements other than buildings (e.g. pier decking replacement on Green Pleasure Pier), machinery and
equipment, vehicles, and infrastructure (e.g. street paving). Capital assets can also include information technology. The
City defines capital assets as assets with an initial cost of more than $5,000 and an expected useful life of at least 5
years.

 Glossary

Glossary
Abatement: A reduction or elimination of a real or personal property tax, motor vehicle excise, a fee, charge, or special
assessment imposed by a governmental unit. Granted only on application of the person seeking the abatement and
only by the committing governmental unit.

Accounting System: The total structure of records and procedures that identify record, classify, and report
information on the financial position and operations of a governmental unit or any of its funds, account groups, and
organizational components.

Accrued Interest: The amount of interest that has accumulated on the debt since the date of the last interest
payment, and on the sale of a bond, the amount accrued up to but not including the date of delivery (settlement
date). (See Interest)

ACFR: Annual Comprehensive Financial Report - A detailed report of an organization's financial activities and
performance over the fiscal year.

Amortization: The gradual repayment of an obligation over time and in accordance with a predetermined payment
schedule.

Appropriation: A legal authorization from the community's legislative body to expend money and incur obligations
for specific public purposes. An appropriation is usually limited in amount and as to the time period within which it
may be expended.

Arbitrage: As applied to municipal debt, the investment of tax-exempt bonds or note proceeds in higher yielding,
taxable securities. Section 103 of the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Code restricts this practice and requires (beyond
certain limits) that earnings be rebated (paid) to the IRS.

Assessed Valuation: A value assigned to real estate or other property by a government as the basis for levying taxes.

Assets: Items owned by an organization that have economic value, such as cash, investments, property, and
equipment.

Available Funds: Balances in the various fund types that represent non-recurring revenue sources. As a matter of

the property owner may request that the assessors apportion the betterment over 20 years. Over the life of the

 Accounting and Financial Reporting

Accounting and Financial Reporting
Purpose:
The purpose of this policy is to ensure the proper recording of financial transactions and identify the parties
responsible for financial reporting.

Background:
The City’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) presents the government and its component units (entities
for which the government is considered to be financially accountable) financial and operating activities. The City's
blended component units, although legally separate entities, are, in substance, part of the City's operations and
financial data from these units are combined with data of the City. The City’s financial statements and accounting
records are maintained in accordance with the recommendations of the Governmental Accounting Standards Board
(GASB).
The government-wide financial statements report information on all of the non-fiduciary activities of the primary
government and its component units. For the most part, the effect of inter-fund activity has been removed from these
statements. Governmental activities, normally supported by taxes and inter-governmental revenues, are reported
separately from business-type activities that rely, to a significant extent, on fees and charges for support.

Separate financial statements are provided for governmental funds, proprietary funds, and fiduciary funds, even
though the latter are excluded from the government-wide financial statements. Major individual governmental funds
are reported as separate columns in the fund financial statements. The government-wide financial statements are
reported using the economic resources measurement focus and the accrual basis of accounting, as are the proprietary
fund and fiduciary fund financial statements. Revenues are recorded when earned and expenses are recorded when a
liability is incurred, regardless of the timing of related cash flows. Property taxes are recognized as revenues in the year
for which they are levied. Grants and similar items are recognized as revenue as soon as all eligibility requirements
imposed by the providers have been met. As a general rule, the effect of inter-fund activity has been eliminated from
the government-wide financial statements. Direct expenses have not been eliminated from the functional categories;
however, indirect expenses and internal payments have been eliminated.

Amounts reported as program revenues include: 1) charges to customers or applicants for goods, services, or privileges
provided; 2) operating grants and contributions; and 3) capital grants and contributions, including special
assessments. Internally dedicated resources are reported as general revenues rather than program revenues. Likewise,
general revenues include all taxes.

Governmental fund financial statements are reported using the current financial resources measurement focus and
the modified accrual basis of accounting. Revenues are recognized as soon as they are both measurable and available.
Revenues are considered available when they are collected within the current period or soon enough thereafter to pay
liabilities of the current period. For this purpose, the City considers revenues available if they are collected within 60
days of the end of the current fiscal period. Expenditures generally are recorded when a liability is incurred, as under
accrual accounting. However, debt service expenditures, as well as expenditures related to compensated absences are
recorded only when payment is due.

Taxes, licenses and interest associated with the current fiscal period are all considered to be susceptible to accrual and
are therefore recognized as revenues of the current fiscal period. Only the portion of special assessments receivable
due within the current fiscal period is considered to be susceptible to accrual as revenue of the current period. All
other revenue items are considered measurable and available only when the City receives cash.

The City reports the following governmental fund types:

  General Fund has been classified as a major fund and is used to account for resources traditionally associated
  with governments which are not required legally or by sound financial management to be accounted for in
  another fund.

  Nonmajor Funds is the aggregate of all the other government funds.

Policy:
Each year an audit will be conducted by an independent Certified Public Accountant Firm (CPA Firm). The selection of
the independent CPA Firm shall be in conformance with the City’s professional services bidding procedures. Generally,
the City shall request bids for audit services no less frequently than every five years. The CPA Firm shall provide the City
Council with an Audit Communication Letter addressing significant findings of the auditors in conjunction with their
opinion on the City’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report. These reports shall be submitted to the City Council
within 60 days of receipt of the report.

During the annual budget process, the City will make available a preliminary year end, unaudited, General Fund fund
balance. It should be recognized, however, that the balance provided is subject to both unforeseen financial
transactions of a material nature and subject to findings of the independent audit. An audit verified year-end balance
should be available by the end of December. The City will use generally accepted accounting principles in preparing
its annual financial statements, and will strive to meet the requirements of the GFOA’s Award for Excellence in
Financial Reporting program.

 Budget Process

Budget Process
Purpose:
The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the preparation, adoption, and presentation of the City’s annual
budget.

Background:
The City of Avalon operates on a fiscal year basis, starting July 1 and ending June 30. The budget is prepared by the
Finance Department with the support of each operating department under the direct supervision of the City
Manager. The Finance Department is responsible for coordinating all revenues estimates contained in the budget.
Estimates are reached by analyzing historical revenue history, national and local economic trends and indices, and
development patterns in the local economy. The Finance Department also coordinates the development of the
expenditure budgets with the support of each operating department and the City Manager.

The budget is structured to separate operating and capital activity at the fund and department level. The operating
budget is a guide for the receipt and disbursement of funds used to provide daily, routine public services to the
community. The operating budget is structured to include historical budget and actual revenues and expenditures,
along with the current revenue estimates and proposed expenditures required in order to implement and maintain
services to the community. The Capital Improvement Program (CIP) budget details the acquisition, construction, or
rehabilitation of major capital facilities and infrastructure over a ten year period.

Policy:
The proposed budget is to be presented to the City Council and community in public workshop meetings in May or
June for review, public input, and deliberation. After providing opportunities for public review and discussion at City
Council workshops and City Council meetings, the budget is adopted by the City Council prior to June 30 at either a
regular or special City Council Meeting. The City Council may amend or supplement the budget at any time after its
adoption by majority vote of the Council Members.

The budget document should incorporate the following guidelines to facilitate broader consumption and greater
comprehension. The document should be organized in a manner that reduces redundancy and allows for a logical
flow of information. The budget document should include an introduction and overview, financial summaries,
operating and capital detail, departmental information, and a glossary. The document should avoid excessive detail,
which can distract from the primary points presented, and should present the information in a consistent manner
across departments and budget years.

 Structurally Balanced Budget

Structurally Balance Budget
Purpose:

The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the City’s operating funds aimed at achieving and maintaining
a structurally balanced budget. State law requires that the City adopts a balanced budget. However, a budget that is
balanced by the state’s definition may not necessarily be structurally balanced or sustainable if recurring expenditures
are covered by reserves or non-recurring or highly volatile revenues. This policy supports the on-going financial
stability of the City by advancing a more sustainable definition of a balanced budget – a structurally balanced budget.

Background:

This section defines key terms related to a structurally balanced budget:

Recurring Revenues are the portion of the City’s revenues that can reasonably be predicted to continue year-to-year,
with some degree of predictability. Property taxes are an example of a recurring revenue. Non-recurring Revenue are
revenues that are one-time in nature and cannot be reasonably expected to continue year-to-year.

Some revenue sources may have both recurring and non-recurring components. These sources require the City to
exercise judgment in determining how much of the source is truly recurring. For example, the City regularly receives
transfer fees for the sale of moorings in the harbor; however, the amount received varies year-to-year based on the
value of moorings and number of sales. In this case, it may be prudent to regard unusually high transfer revenues as
non-recurring revenue under the assumption that such revenues are unlikely to continue, making it imprudent to use
them for recurring expenditures.

Recurring expenditures appear in the budget each year. Salaries, benefits, rent, utilities, maintenance costs and
certain contracted services are common examples of recurring expenditures. In general, recurring expenditures
should be those that the City expects to fund every year in order to maintain current service levels. Non-recurring
expenditures comprise special projects such as capital improvements, asset acquisitions, and other costs incurred
infrequently by the City. In general, the City has a greater degree of flexibility to defer non-recurring expenditures than
recurring ones.

Reserves are the portion of fund balance set aside as a hedge against risk. The City has defined a minimum amount
of funds it will hold in reserve. This serves as a “bottom line measure” to help determine the extent to which the City’s
structural balance policy is being met – if reserves are maintained at their desired levels, it is an indication that the City
is maintaining a structurally balanced budget. If reserves are declining, it may indicate an imbalance in the budget
(e.g. if reserves are being used to fund on-going expenditures). Desired reserve levels are further discussed in Sections
F and G of this document.

Policy:

The City shall endeavor to adopt a structurally balanced budget. Generally, this means that recurring expenditures
should be covered by recurring revenues and that non-recurring revenues should be used to fund non-recurring
expenditures. The Finance Department shall incorporate information into its budget presentation demonstrating the
City’s progress in achieving a structurally balanced budget.

In order to achieve a structurally balanced budget, the City should consider the following:

  Employee compensation and non-recurring revenues – With limited exceptions, non-recurring revenues and
  reserves should not be used to fund employee compensation. One such exception might be a severe economic
  downturn where non-recurring revenues are temporarily used to ease the transition to an expenditure structure

  Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Proposed Operating and Capital Budget | Avalon  Page 287

  that is in line with new economic realities. Even this should only be done in the context of a plan to return to
  structural balance and replenish any reserves that had been used.
  Operating and maintenance costs of capital assets purchased with non-recurring revenues – While capital assets
  are often funded with non-recurring revenues, the City shall be observant of the long-term operating and
  maintenance costs of such purposes, to prevent the creation of new on-going expenditures that cannot be
  maintained by recurring revenues.
  Replacement of short-lived assets and non-recurring revenues – The City shall prioritize the use of non-recurring
  revenues to replace current assets that have outlived their useful lives over the purchase of entirely new assets,
  where the replacement of the expired or obsolete assets is critical to the maintenance of the City’s core
  programs. A replacement schedule for such assets is a good indicator of when to budget for these items.

 Revenue Policy

Revenue Policy
Purpose:

The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for (a) the development of revenue estimates, (b) fee structures,
and (c) use of new recurring and non-recurring revenues in order to achieve a structurally balanced budget.

Background:

Revenue projections and assumptions are critical to budget decisions, particularly in order to achieve a structurally
balanced budget. The Finance Department is responsible for coordinating all revenues estimates contained in the
budget. Estimates are reached by analyzing historical revenue history, national and local economic trends and indices,
and development patterns in the local economy. Many of the City’s key revenues are subject to significant fluctuation
dependent on a number of economic factors. While it is difficult to always achieve accurate projections in a dynamic
economic environment, it is important to have a consistent approach to projecting revenues in order for decision-
makers to understand the basis used to project the resources available for the budget. Revenue should be projected in
a way that is not likely to lead to a revenue shortfall, but also not to be so conservative that the projections consistently
and substantially underestimate revenues.

The City utilizes user charges and fees to help fund services. When certain services provided especially benefit a
particular group, the City should consider charges and fees on the direct recipients of those that receive benefits for
such services. The City may elect to subsidize a service for various reasons, including the ability of residents or
businesses to pay; however, the City should have a documented rationale regarding why the full cost is not recovered.

By definition, non-recurring revenues cannot be relied upon in future budget periods. Non-recurring revenues include
the sales of government assets, infrequent revenues from development and grants.

Policy:

The following guidelines are to be considered with regards to City revenues:

  a. Development of Revenue Estimates - The City will estimate revenues using an objective and analytical process,
  with a conservative approach adopted to address any uncertainties. The approach should result in overall
  budgeted revenues for a fund being set at a level such that it is unlikely that actual revenues are lower than

Expenditure Controls
Purpose:

The purpose of this policy is to provide outline appropriation and expenditure controls designed to safeguard limited
government assets and ensure that resources are maintained where they were originally approved during the budget
process.

Background:

The budget document serves as a plan of financial operation, identifying adopted appropriations as well as the
specific types and levels of services to be provided. Appropriations are made by City Council at the fund level, with
expenditures grouped into the following major categories:

  Personnel – Expenditures related to labor including salaries, overtime, worker’s compensation, health, insurance,
  and retirement benefits
  Maintenance and Operations – Expenditures for items which primarily benefit the current period and are not
  defined as personnel, contract services, or capital outlays.
  Contract Services – Expenditures rendered to a government by private firms, individuals, or other government
  agencies.
  Capital Outlays – Expenditures that result in the acquisition of, or addition to, fixed assets that are tangible,
  durable, non-consumable, costs $5,000 or more, and have a useful life of more than one year.

Department heads and their designated representatives may authorize expenditures that are based on appropriations
previously authorized by City Council action, generally through the adopted budget, and only from accounts under
their organizational responsibility. Individual transactions are classified by departments at the account level, with the
most appropriate account used to classify the expenditure. During the course of the year, departments may encounter
necessary and unanticipated expenditures that are able to be covered through budget savings in other accounts
under their control. These budget transfers allow the City to operate more efficiently with the implementation of
controls to ensure the budget goals are still met with the approved appropriations.

City Council approval is required for any budget revisions or amendments that increase the total amount appropriated

General Fund Reserves
Purpose:

The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the General Fund’s unrestricted fund balance to improve and
maintain the City’s financial stability in order to protect the City from unforeseen or unbudgeted situations (e.g.
natural disasters, major infrastructure failures, unexpected litigation).

Background:

Fund balance serves as a measure of the financial resources available in a governmental fund. It is essential that
governments maintain adequate levels of fund balance to mitigate current and future risks (e.g. revenue shortfalls and
unanticipated expenditures) and to ensure stable tax rates.

In February 2009, the Governmental Accounting Standards Board issued GASB Statement No. 54, Fund Balance
Reporting and Governmental Fund Type Definitions, which separates fund balance into five separate categories based
on the type and source of constraints placed on how resources can be spent. Presented in descending order from
most constraining to least constraining, they include: nonspendable fund balance, restricted fund balance, committed
fund balance, assigned fund balance, and unassigned fund balance. The total amounts in the last three categories
(where the only constraint on spending, if any, is imposed by the government itself) is termed unrestricted fund
balance. GASB Statement No. 54 recommends “…at a minimum, that general-purpose governments, regardless of size,
maintain unrestricted fund balance in their general fund of no less than two months of regular general fund operating
revenues or regular general fund operating expenditures. The choice of revenues or expenditures as a basis of
comparison may be dictated by what is more predictable in a government’s particular circumstances.”

The adequacy of unrestricted fund balance in the General Fund should take into account the City’s unique
circumstances and the City should consider the following factors to assess the adequacy of unrestricted fund balance:

  Predictability of its revenues and volatility of its expenditures;
  Perceived exposure to significant one-time outlays;
  Potential drain upon General Fund resources from other funds, as well as the availability of resources in other
  funds;
  Potential impact on the entity’s bond ratings and the corresponding increased cost of borrowed funds;
  Commitments and assignments included in the unrestricted fund balance

Policy:

The City of Avalon will strive to maintain an unrestricted fund balance equal to no less than six (6) months of regular
General Fund operating expenditure budget. The regular operating expenditure budget includes all current operating
expenditure appropriations, excluding capital outlays and other one-time discretionary payments.

Visitor-driven tax revenues (e.g. transient occupancy tax, sales tax, admission tax) account for the majority of the City’s
General Fund revenues, with the predictability of these revenues dependent on overall tourism demand. Due to its
unique location, City revenues are particularly vulnerable to disruptions to leisure travel and tourism caused by
pandemics or other natural disasters. In addition, the City is responsible for managing multiple enterprise funds, with
operating expenditures comparable in size to its General Fund, and the City needs to maintain reserves in order to
cover immediate capital needs, if working capital is not sufficient in those funds.

Funds appropriated from unrestricted fund balance should be appropriated for non-recurring expenditures, as they
represent prior year surpluses that may or may not materialize in subsequent years. However, draws from unrestricted
fund balance below the six month target amount or to cover recurring operating costs are generally reserved for

situations may include but not limited to the following:

  A. Sudden and unexpected significant facility failure that presents an immediate public safety concern to the

Enterprise Fund Working Capital Targets
Purpose:

The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the enterprise funds’ working capital target to improve and
maintain the City’s financial stability in order to protect the City from unforeseen or unbudgeted situations (e.g.
natural disasters, major infrastructure failures, unexpected litigation).

Background:

Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) does not permit the reporting of fund balance for enterprise funds.
However, enterprise funds distinguish between current and non-current assets and liabilities, allowing for the
calculation of working capital (i.e. current assets less current liabilities). Working capital indicates the relatively liquid
portion of total enterprise fund capital, which constitutes a margin or buffer for meeting obligations. For all further
references to reserves for enterprise funds, net working capital is the intended meaning.

It is essential that a government maintain adequate levels of reserves or working capital in enterprise funds to
mitigate current and future risks (e.g., revenue shortfalls and unanticipated expenses) and to ensure stable services
and fees. Strength of collection practices, historical consumption of inventories, support from the general government,
transfers out, cash cycles, customer concentration, demand for services, control over rates and revenues, asset age and
condition, volatility of expenses, control over expenses, management plans for working capital and debt position
should all be considered in determining adequate working capital or reserve targets for each fund.

Policy:

The City’s Enterprise Funds include the Harbor Fund, Sewer Fund, Saltwater Fund, Solid Waste Fund, and Avalon
Transit Fund. Reserve levels for each fund are as follows:

  Harbor Fund - The City of Avalon will strive to maintain a working capital balance equal to no less than four (4)
  months of regular Harbor Fund operating expenditure budget to cover harbor operations (Fund 103) and a
  minimum reserve of five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000) to provide funding to cover emergency capital
  costs in the harbor (Fund 104). The reserve amount exceeds the GFOA’s 45-day minimum working capital
  recommendation due to the Harbor’s limited ability to reduce variable costs in response to lower revenues (i.e.
  public safety costs relatively fixed), customer concentration (i.e. majority of revenues paid by cross channel and
  cruise ship carriers), and condition of infrastructure.
  Sewer Fund – The City of Avalon will strive to maintain a target reserve balance equal to no less than three (3)
  months of operating and maintenance expenses, as outlined in the cost of service study. The reserve amount
  exceeds the GFOA’s 45-day minimum working capital recommendation due to the cash cycle, with remittances
  concentrated in the second half of the fiscal year, and condition of infrastructure.
  Saltwater Fund – The City of Avalon will strive to maintain a target reserve balance equal to no less than three (3)
  months of operating and maintenance expenses, as outlined in the cost of service study. The reserve amount
  exceeds the GFOA’s 45-day minimum working capital recommendation due to the cash cycle, with remittances
  concentrated in the second half of the fiscal year, and condition of infrastructure.
  Solid Waste Fund – The City of Avalon will strive to maintain a target reserve balance equal to no less than three
  (3) months of operating and maintenance expenses, as outlined in the cost of service study. The reserve amount
  exceeds the GFOA’s 45-day minimum working capital recommendation due to the cash cycle, with remittances
  concentrated in the second half of the fiscal year, and condition of infrastructure.
  Avalon Transit Fund – The Avalon Transit Fund is subsidized by the General Fund, as transit revenues are not
  sufficient to cover operations. No working capital target has been set for this fund as the financial buffer or
  cushion is provided by the General Fund.

Investment Policy
Policy:

It is the policy of the City of Avalon and the Successor Agency to the ACIA (hereinafter collectively referred to as
"City" or the City of Avalon") to invest public funds in a prudent manner which will provide in the following order; 1)
the highest level of safety of funds, along with 2) liquidity of funds in order that
daily cash flow demands are met and, finally, that 3) yield or investment return be maximized while conforming to all
laws of the State of California regarding the investment of public funds.

In accordance with Section 53646 ofthe government Code, the Finance Director and City Treasurer
will annually render to the City Council a Statement of Investment Policy. The Finance Director,
City Treasurer, and City Manager shall review the policy on an annual basis for submission and approval
by the City Council.

Scope:

The City/Agency Treasurer (hereinafter referred to as "Treasurer") is authorized to invest the City's
funds in accordance with the California Government Code Sections 53601.1,53602, and 53635. This
investment policy applies to all financial assets of the City of Avalon. These funds are accounted for in the City’s
Comprehensive Annual Financial Report, which includes the following fund types:

  GeneralFund
  Special revenue
  Debt Service
  Capital Projects
  Enterprise
  InternalService
  Trust and Agency
  Any new fund created by the legislative body, unless specifically exempted

All monies entrusted to the Treasurer will be pooled in an actively managed portfolio except for the employee's
retirement funds, which are administered separately and the proceeds of certain debt issues, which are managed
and invested by trustees appointed under indenture agreements.

Prudence:

The actions of the Treasurer in the performance of his or her duties as manager of public funds shall
be evaluated using the following prudent person standard applied in the context of managing the overall portfolio:

  Investments shall be made with judgment and care, under circumstances then prevailing, which persons of
  prudence, discretion, and intelligence exercise in the management of their own affairs, not for
  speculation, but for investment, considering the probable safety of their capital as well as
  the probable income to be derived.
  Investment officers acting in accordance with written procedures and the investment policy exercising
  due diligence shall be relieved of personal responsibility for an individual security's credit risk or market
  price changes, provided deviations from expectations are reported in a timely fashion and appropriate
  action is taken to control adverse developments.

Objective:

 Investment Policy

The primary objectives, in priority order, of the City's investment activities shall be:

  1. Safety — Safety of principal is the foremost objective of the investment program. Investments of the City shall
  be undertaken in a manner that seeks to ensure the preservation of capital in the overall
  portfolio. The City shall seek to safeguard principal by a careful examination of credit risk and market risk of
  individual investments.
  a. Credit Risk — The chance that an issuer will be unable to
  make scheduled payments of interest and principal on an outstanding obligation. Another concern for
  investors is that the market's perceptions of a corporation's credit will cause the market value of a
  security to fall, even if default is not expected.
  i. Market Risk — The chance that the value of a security will decline as interest rates rise. In general, as
  interest rates fall, prices of fixed income securities rise. Similarly, as interest rates rise, prices fall.
  Market risk is also referred to as systematic risk or risk that affects all securities within an asset class
  similarly.
  2. Liquidity - The City investment portfolio will remain sufficiently liquid to enable the City to meet all operating
  expenditure requirements, which might be reasonably anticipated. In order to maintain liquidity,
  no more than 50 percent of the portfolio will have a maturity in excess of one (1) year.
  3. Return on Investment — The City investment portfolio shall be designed with the objective of
  attaining a market rate of return throughout budgetary and economic cycles, taking
  into account the City investment risk constraints and the cash flow characteristics of the portfolio. Whenever
  possible, consistent with risk limitations and prudent investment principles, the City shall make an effort to
  achieve returns at the market average rate of return. The market average rate of return is defined as
  the average return on six-month US Treasury Bills.

Delegation of Authority:

The Treasurer has been authorized to undertake investment transactions on behalf of the City. This authority shall
not pass to the Deputy Treasurer unless specifically authorized in writing by the Treasurer. Although the
Treasurer has been authorized to undertake investment transactions, management
responsibility for the City's investment program has been delegated to the Finance Department. The only officials
authorized to undertake investment transactions on behalf of the City are the Treasurer, Finance Director,
and City Manager. The actual disbursement of funds for the placement of individual investments
undertaken by these three officials shall be subject to second party approval
by officers authorized to sign City checks and wire transfers: the Mayor, City Manager, Chief
Administrative Officer,and certain Department Heads.

The Treasurer is responsible for ensuring compliance with the City's investment policies and for ensuring that strong
internal controls are in place through the oversight of the Finance Director.

Officers and employees involved in the investment process shall refrain from personal business activity that
could conflict with proper execution of the investment program, or which could impair their ability to make
impartial investment decisions. The Treasurer, Finance Director, and all investment employees are
required to file annual disclosure statements as required by the Fair Political Practices Commission (FPPC), thus shall
disclose to the City Clerk any material financial interests in financial institutions that conduct business
within the jurisdiction, and they shall further disclose any large personal financial investment positions
that could be related to the performance of the City investment portfolio.

Glossary:

Bankers' Acceptance - A draft bill or exchange accepted by a bank or trust company. The accepting institution,
as well as the issuer, guarantees payment of the bill.
Bonds - A debt obligation of a firm or public entity. A bond represents the agreement to repay the debt in principle
and, typically, in interest on the principal.
Broker - A person or firm that acts as an intermediary by purchasing and selling securities for others rather than for
his or its own account.
Cash Flow — A comparison of cash receipts (revenues) to required payments(debt service, operating expenses, etc.).
Certificate of Deposit — A short-term, secured deposit in a financial institution that usually returns principal
and interest to the lender at the end of the loan period. Certificates of Deposit (CDs) differ in terms of
collateralization and marketability. Those appropriate to public agency investing include Negotiable
Certificates of Deposit and Non-Negotiable Certificates of Deposit.
Collateralization - Process by which a borrower pledges securities, property, or other deposits for the
purpose of securing the repayment of a loan and/or security.
Coupon — The annual rate of interest that a bond's issuer promises to pay the bondholder on the bond's face value; a
certificate attached to a bond evidencing interest due on a payment date.
Dealer — Someone who acts as a principal in all transactions, including underwriting, buying, and selling securities,
including from his/her own account.
Discount — The difference between the par value of a security and the cost of the security, when the cost is
below par. Investors purchase securities at a discount when the return to the investor (yield) is
higher than the stated coupon (interest rate) on the investment.
Diversification — Dividing investment funds among a variety of securities offering independent return.
Federal Credit Agencies — Agencies of the Federal Government set up to supply credit to various classes
of institutions and individuals (e.g. savings and loans,small business firms, students, farmers, farm cooperatives, and
exporters).
Federal deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) — A Federal agency that insures bank deposits,
currently up to $250,000 per institution.
Fiduciary — An individual who holds something in trust for another and bears liability for its safekeeping.
Liquidity — The measure of the ability to convert an instrument to cash on a given date at full face or par value.
Local Agency Investment Fund — A voluntary investment fund open to government entities and certain non-profit
organizations in California that is manage by the State Treasurer's Office.
Local Government Investment Pool — Investment pools that range from the State Treasurer's Office Local
Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) to county pools, to Joint PowersAuthorities (JPAs). These funds are not subject

  Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Proposed Operating and Capital Budget | Avalon  Page 301

to the same SEC rules applicable to money market mutual funds.
Market Value — The price at which a security is trading and presumably could be purchased or sold at a particular
point in time.
Maturity — The date on which the principal or stated value of an investment becomes due and payable.
Money Market Mutual Funds - Mutual funds that invest exclusively in short-term money market instruments. MMF's
seek the preservation of capital as a primary goal while maintaining a high degree of liquidity and providing
income representative of the market for short-term investments.
Municipal Notes, Bonds, and Other Obligations — Obligations issued by state and local governments to
finance capital and operating expenses.
Mutual Funds — An investment company that pools money and can invest in a variety of securities, including fixed-
income securities and money market instruments.
Portfolio — Combined holding of more than one stock, bond, commodity, real estate investment,
cash equivalent, or other asset. The purpose of a portfolio is to reduce risk by diversification.
Prudent Person Standard — A standard of conduct where a person acts with care, skill, prudence, and
